questions.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
questions.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
questions.question: A risk analyst is classifying four trades by arbitrage type. Which of the following pairings is correct?

options.text: Shorting the on-the-run 30-year Treasury while buying the cheaper off-the-run 29.5-year issue is relative value arbitrage.
Buying one stock and shorting a peer whose price relationship has temporarily diverged without fundamental news is relative value arbitrage.
Buying a target company's stock and shorting the acquirer's stock in a share-for-share deal is convertible arbitrage.
Buying a convertible bond and shorting the underlying stock to neutralise equity exposure is fixed-income arbitrage.

questions.solution:
Arbitrage strategies look for situations in which the same asset trades at different prices in different markets, two assets with similar cash flows are priced differently, or an asset with a known future price trades today at a value not reflecting its risk-free discounted price.

| Family | Identifying trade | What convergence is expected |
|---|---|---|
| Fixed-income arbitrage | Short the expensive on-the-run 30-year Treasury, buy the cheaper off-the-run 29.5-year issue. Also, divergence between U.S. Treasury yields and hedged yields on Italian government bonds. | The on-the-run liquidity premium fades over time, producing small positive profits. |
| Convertible arbitrage | Buy the convertible bond, short the underlying stock. | Income plus monetised volatility; the equity risk is hedged away rather than bet on. |
| Relative value arbitrage | Pairs trading between competitors or peers whose historically strong price correlation has temporarily diverged. Also index futures against their constituents, and statistical arbitrage across many positions. | The spread reverts to its prior relationship. |
| Merger arbitrage, or risk arbitrage, an event-driven strategy | Buy the target's stock and, in share-for-share deals, short the acquirer's stock. | The spread between the post-announcement price and the offer price closes if the deal completes. |

a.reason: The trade is correctly described but it is the textbook example of fixed-income arbitrage, not relative value.

b.reason: Pairs trading is the long-established relative value arbitrage strategy, and the qualifier "without any fundamental news" is what makes the divergence a mispricing rather than information.

c.reason: Correctly describes merger arbitrage, an event-driven strategy, then labels it convertible arbitrage.

d.reason: Correctly describes convertible arbitrage, then labels it fixed-income arbitrage. The label is superficially defensible because a convertible is a bond, which is what makes this the strongest distractor.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP in all three wrong options, each pairing an accurate trade description with a neighbouring label. Nothing can be eliminated on the description, so the discrimination is entirely in the label, and option (d) is the one to watch because the instrument class supports the wrong answer. Discriminator worth logging: the family is named for the source of the mispricing, not for the asset class traded. A convertible bond traded against its own equity is a volatility and conversion-option trade, which is why it gets its own family.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
questions.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
questions.question: Which of the following characteristics best defines a convertible arbitrage strategy?

options.text: Buying undervalued sovereign bonds and shorting corporate bonds.
Taking offsetting long and short positions across different yield curves.
Buying a convertible bond and shorting the underlying stock to hedge equity exposure.
Buying stocks with high dividend yields while shorting stocks with relatively low dividend yields.

questions.solution:
A convertible bond contains an embedded equity call option. The holder may convert into a specified number of shares and will do so when the share value received exceeds the bond's cash redemption value, and until then continues to receive coupons like a traditional bondholder. Its price is sensitive to three things.

| Sensitivity | Corresponding value component | Handled in the arbitrage by |
|---|---|---|
| Changes in interest rates | Investment value | Retained, and compensated by the coupon |
| Issuer's credit risk | Investment value | Retained; this is a genuine exposure of the strategy |
| Issuer's share price and its volatility | Conversion value and option value | Hedged by shorting the underlying stock in the delta-implied quantity |

So the strategy buys the convertible and simultaneously sells short the underlying stock, seeking to profit from both the bond's income and equity volatility while neutralising directional equity risk. The hedge is not static: as the share price moves, the delta of the convertible changes, requiring continuous rebalancing, a process known as delta hedging.

a.reason: Describes a credit or sovereign spread trade, which sits within fixed-income arbitrage. No convertible instrument is involved.

b.reason: Describes a yield-curve or cross-market fixed-income arbitrage trade, such as the Treasury against hedged Italian government bond example.

c.reason: Both legs named and the purpose of the short leg stated correctly.

d.reason: Describes a dividend-yield factor trade, which is a relative value or equity style strategy. Dividends appear in convertible arbitrage only as a cost, since the arbitrageur must pay dividends to the stock lender on the borrowed shares.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP across the arbitrage families again, with (a) and (b) both drawn from fixed-income arbitrage. Option (d) is the more interesting distractor because dividends genuinely do feature in convertible arbitrage, just on the wrong side of the ledger: they are an expense paid to the lender, not a return sought. Whenever an option names a real component of the strategy, check which side of the profit and loss it sits on.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
questions.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
questions.question: A convertible arbitrage manager explains to an investor that beyond the bond's coupon and the interest on short sale proceeds, the trade has a further source of return described as monetising volatility. Which of the following best explains that source?

options.text: Because the relationship between the stock price and the convertible bond price is nonlinear, a move in the stock in either direction tends to produce a gain on the hedged position, since the gain on one leg exceeds the loss on the other.
Because the delta hedge is set once at inception and left unchanged, the position accumulates option premium in the same way as a short straddle.
Because the convertible bond's implied volatility is systematically higher than the realised volatility of the underlying stock, the manager earns the volatility risk premium.
Because the short stock position is rebalanced continuously, transaction costs are converted into a positive carry once the borrow fee falls below the coupon.

questions.solution:
The delta hedge neutralises the first-order sensitivity of the convertible to the share price. It cannot neutralise the second-order sensitivity, because the short stock position is linear in the share price while the convertible is not.

| Share price move | Convertible bond | Short stock hedge |
|---|---|---|
| Rises | Gains, and gains at an accelerating rate as the embedded call moves toward the money | Loses linearly |
| Falls | Loses, but at a decelerating rate as the bond floor approaches | Gains linearly |

In both directions the convex leg outperforms the linear leg, so the hedged position gains on a move of either sign. The source describes the effect as an asymmetry: changes in the stock price affect the hedge asymmetrically. When the stock falls, the gain on the short stock exceeds the loss on the convertible; when it rises, the gain on the convertible exceeds the loss on the short stock. (Stowell's own sentence, that the gain or loss on the short stock tends to exceed the corresponding loss or gain on the convertible, holds only for a falling stock. Recognise that wording if it appears in an exam option, but the mechanism is that the convex leg wins in both directions.) It is likened to the convexity observed in the bond price and yield relationship.

The economic consequence is that a delta-hedged convertible is a long volatility position. The larger the realised movement in the stock, the more the rebalancing captures. A separate and independent source of return arises when the convertible itself is undervalued, for instance when the embedded call is priced below fair value.

a.reason: Names nonlinearity as the mechanism, states that the effect works in both directions, and identifies the asymmetry between the two legs.

b.reason: Wrong on both the mechanic and the sign. The hedge requires continuous rebalancing rather than being set once, and a delta-hedged convertible is long volatility, which is the opposite of a short straddle.

c.reason: Describes the volatility risk premium earned by option sellers. The convertible holder is long the embedded call, so a systematic excess of implied over realised volatility would work against the position rather than for it.

d.reason: Transaction costs and borrow fees are costs of the strategy and are not converted into carry by rebalancing. Rebalancing frequency raises transaction costs, which is a genuine drag on the volatility harvest rather than a source of it.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (b) and (c), both placing the manager on the short volatility side when the position is long volatility, and (c) is the more dangerous because the volatility risk premium is a real and heavily tested concept elsewhere in the syllabus. The check is direction of exposure: the arbitrageur owns a bond containing a call, so the arbitrageur is long optionality and therefore long volatility. SIBLING SWAP at (d), converting a cost line into a return line.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
questions.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
questions.question: A company has issued bonds convertible into equity after three years. Because of an error in the conversion factor, the convertible bonds appear undervalued relative to the projected market price of the company's stock at conversion. A hedge fund manager wants to exploit the trading opportunity created by this underestimation. The most appropriate strategy is:

options.text: going short the convertible security and long the common stock.
going short the convertible security and short the common stock.
going long the convertible security and short the common stock.
going long the common stock and long the convertible security.

questions.solution:
**Step 1.** Identify what is mispriced. The convertible is undervalued. The stock is not stated to be mispriced. So the trade must be long the cheap instrument.

**Step 2.** Identify what must be hedged. Owning the convertible brings equity exposure through the embedded call. The manager's view is on the conversion factor, not on the direction of the share price, so that equity exposure is unwanted and is hedged by shorting the underlying stock in the delta-implied quantity.

$$\text{Position: long convertible bond} + \text{short (delta} \times \text{conversion ratio) shares}$$

This is the canonical structure. The index definition used by convertible arbitrage funds states it plainly: the funds aim to profit from purchasing convertible securities and subsequently shorting the corresponding stock when there is a pricing error in the conversion factor of the security.

a.reason: Exactly inverted. Shorting the undervalued instrument and buying the fairly priced one loses money as the mispricing corrects.

b.reason: Shorts the cheap instrument and, by also shorting the stock, doubles the directional bet rather than hedging it. Both legs are wrong.

c.reason: Long the undervalued convertible, short the stock to neutralise the equity leg.

d.reason: Gets the convertible leg right and then adds equity exposure instead of removing it. The position becomes a levered bullish bet on the share price, and the mispricing in the conversion factor is no longer isolated.

trap.explanation: SIGN ERROR at (a) and (b) on the convertible leg, and a POLARITY FLIP at (d) on the hedge leg. Option (d) is the instructive one, because the reasoning behind it is not absurd: if the convertible is cheap relative to a projected share price, buying both instruments looks like doubling down on the same view. It is not, because the view is about the relationship between the two prices, not about the level of either. Isolating a relative mispricing always requires opposite signs on the two legs.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Identify reasons for the failures of hedge funds in the past
questions.reading: Reading 94: Due Diligence for Hedge Funds
questions.question: An investor is compiling a checklist of the reasons hedge funds have failed in the past, so as to avoid investing in a failing fund. Each of the following appears on the standard list EXCEPT which one?

options.text: Excess leverage, which magnifies losses as readily as it magnifies gains
Lack of liquidity, where simultaneous withdrawals create a cash-flow squeeze the fund cannot meet
Excessive concentration of the manager's personal wealth in the fund, which distorts the manager's incentives toward risk aversion
Poor controls, where a lack of supervision permits risk taking large enough to bankrupt the fund

questions.solution:
The eight reasons. Reference list.

| Reason | Detail |
|---|---|
| 1. Poor investment decisions | Either a series of decisions producing a domino effect, or a single calculated risk that backfired. |
| 2. Fraud | Accounting fraud such as misstating asset book values or income; valuation fraud such as misstating market values; and outright theft of funds. |
| 3. Extreme events | Events that would otherwise occur with very low probability, or that were simply unexpected, such as market crashes. |
| 4. Excess leverage | Related to poor investment decisions. Leverage goes both ways: it magnifies gains and equally magnifies losses. |
| 5. Lack of liquidity | Too many withdrawals and redemptions at once, creating a cash-flow squeeze and an inability to meet them all. |
| 6. Poor controls | Closely related to fraud. Lack of supervision permits excessive risk taking large enough to bankrupt the fund. |
| 7. Insufficient questioning | In committee decision making, a dominant member sways the decision or members are afraid to raise valid concerns. All due diligence team members should be encouraged to play devil's advocate and raise concerns early, before the committee stage. |
| 8. Insufficient attention to returns | Funds reducing operational risk sometimes overcompensate with excessive controls, bearing too many expenses and not generating enough return. |

Options (a), (b) and (d) are reasons 4, 5 and 6 respectively, each stated in the source's own terms.

Option (c) inverts a well-established principle. Where an investor is concerned about the asymmetry of risk sharing inherent in hedge fund compensation, since the manager takes a share of profits without a symmetric share of losses, the standard remedy is to verify that the manager has a substantial portion of their own assets invested in the fund. Personal capital at risk aligns the manager with the investor. It is a due diligence check to perform, not a warning sign to avoid.

Two adjacent facts from the same material, both testable. Diversifying a manager's own capital across several strategies fails as a protection at times of stress, when correlations across strategies converge. And investing with a fund that has multiple managers mitigates the risk that an unsuccessful manager closes the fund and reopens under a new name, since a single manager's failed bet is less likely to end the whole vehicle.

a.reason: Reason 4 on the list, with the two-way property of leverage stated correctly.

b.reason: Reason 5, and the mechanism is described accurately.

c.reason: Not on the list, and the direction is inverted. Manager co-investment is the recommended alignment mechanism.

d.reason: Reason 6, closely related to fraud, which is reason 2.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (c) on a governance mechanism, and the justification clause does the concealing work: "distorts the manager's incentives toward risk aversion" sounds like a sophisticated agency argument. It is exactly backwards for this syllabus, where the concern is that managers take too much risk because they share the upside without sharing the downside. Check whether the stated incentive problem is the one the reading actually worries about.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Identify reasons for the failures of hedge funds in the past
questions.reading: Reading 94: Due Diligence for Hedge Funds
questions.question: A due diligence team is reviewing why its own process failed to identify problems at a fund that subsequently collapsed. A junior analyst had reservations about the manager's valuation policy but did not raise them, because the committee chair had already expressed strong support for the investment. Which reason for hedge fund failure does this most closely illustrate, and what is the appropriate remedy?

options.text: Poor controls; the remedy is to increase the frequency of external audit.
Insufficient questioning; the remedy is to encourage all due diligence team members to play devil's advocate and raise concerns early, before the committee stage.
Fraud; the remedy is to require independent third-party valuation of all fund assets.
Insufficient attention to returns; the remedy is to weight the committee toward members with investment rather than operational backgrounds.

questions.solution:
Reason 7 describes exactly this situation: in a committee-style decision-making process there may be a dominant member who sways the decision, or members who are afraid to voice valid concerns over information they have discovered that would question the merits of the manager or the investment.

| Element of the vignette | Match to the stated reason |
|---|---|
| Committee-style decision | The setting the reason specifies |
| Chair had expressed strong support | The dominant member who sways the decision |
| Analyst held reservations but stayed silent | A member afraid to voice a valid concern about information discovered |

The prescribed remedy is equally specific: all due diligence team members should be encouraged to play the role of devil's advocate when appropriate, and to raise reasonable concerns as early as possible, especially before they reach the committee stage. The timing clause matters, because once a view has been voiced by a dominant member in committee, the social cost of dissent is already high.

Note where this failure sits. Most items on the eight-reason list describe something going wrong inside the fund. Insufficient questioning describes something going wrong inside the investor. That distinction is a natural discriminator for an exam item.

a.reason: Poor controls refers to a lack of supervision within the fund allowing excessive risk taking. Nothing in the vignette concerns the fund's internal supervision, and external audit frequency would not have caused the analyst to speak up.

b.reason: Both the diagnosis and the remedy match the source, including the before-the-committee-stage timing.

c.reason: The analyst's reservation concerned a valuation policy. Nothing establishes that any misstatement occurred, and independent valuation, while sound practice, addresses a different failure.

d.reason: Insufficient attention to returns describes a fund that overcompensates with excessive controls and generates too little return. It is unrelated to committee dynamics, and the proposed remedy would if anything worsen the groupthink problem by narrowing the range of perspectives.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP at (a), between poor controls and insufficient questioning, which are genuinely adjacent since both are governance failures. The discriminator is whose governance failed: poor controls is the fund's, insufficient questioning is the investor's. Options (c) and (d) each attach a plausible remedy to the wrong diagnosis, which is the two-part conjunction format; verify the diagnosis first, because a correct-sounding remedy attached to a wrong cause is still wrong.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Identify reasons for the failures of hedge funds in the past
questions.reading: Reading 94: Due Diligence for Hedge Funds
questions.question: A fund manager, responding to investor concern about operational risk, implements an extensive control framework: additional compliance staff, a second independent valuation agent, daily reconciliation across three systems, and pre-approval requirements for all trades above a low threshold. Two years later the fund closes, having generated returns well below its peers while never suffering an operational loss. Which reason for hedge fund failure does this best illustrate?

options.text: Poor controls, since the framework evidently failed to protect the fund's viability.
Insufficient attention to returns, since the fund overcompensated for operational risk and bore too many expenses to generate adequate returns.
Poor investment decisions, since underperformance against peers necessarily reflects a series of flawed investment choices.
Extreme events, since a two-year period of peer underperformance without operational loss is a low-probability outcome.

questions.solution:
Investment funds attempting to reduce operational risk sometimes overcompensate by implementing excessive controls, and may end up bearing too many expenses and not generating enough returns. The stated ideal is a healthy balance between generating strong returns and taking on a reasonable level of risk.

| Evidence in the vignette | What it rules in or out |
|---|---|
| Never suffered an operational loss | Rules out poor controls. The control framework worked exactly as intended. |
| Extensive and duplicative control apparatus | Rules in excessive expense: extra staff, a second valuation agent, triple reconciliation, low pre-approval threshold. |
| Pre-approval on all trades above a low threshold | Adds an opportunity cost beyond expense, since it slows execution and constrains the manager's ability to act on views. |

This is the direct counterpart of Q3 in LO 1: an organisation puts its targets at risk whenever risk capital is used in amounts inconsistent with policy, and that includes using too little. Here the fund suppressed operational risk so thoroughly that it could not earn its cost base.

a.reason: Polarity flip. The fund's problem was too many controls, not too few, and the absence of any operational loss is direct evidence that the controls functioned.

b.reason: Matches reason 8 in both diagnosis and mechanism.

c.reason: Assumes underperformance must be caused by bad investment choices. The vignette locates the cause in the expense base and the operating constraints, and offers no evidence of flawed investment decisions. The word "necessarily" also overreaches.

d.reason: Extreme events means low-probability market outcomes such as crashes. Sustained underperformance driven by a known and self-imposed cost structure is the opposite of an unforeseeable event.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (a), which is the trap this item is built around: the word "controls" appears throughout the vignette, and a candidate pattern-matching on vocabulary rather than on direction will select it. The single fact that settles it is that no operational loss occurred. SCOPE ERROR at (c) and (d), each stretching a real list item to cover a case it does not describe. Reason 8 is the one to rehearse deliberately, because a list of eight recited from memory almost always loses this one first.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
questions.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
questions.question: Which of the following statements about Madoff's reported split-strike conversion strategy is INCORRECT?

options.text: Part of the strategy involved selling an out-of-the-money call option.
A floor value was created by purchasing an out-of-the-money put option.
A long position in a portfolio of stocks highly correlated with the S&P 100 was required.
Gains on the equity portfolio were supplemented by gains on a long out-of-the-money call option position.

questions.solution:
Madoff described his approach as a split-strike conversion, which is a combination of a protective put and a covered call, known to option traders as a collar or bull spread. It is sometimes called a vacation trade, because once established the position typically requires little attention until the options near expiration.

| Step | Position | Effect on the payoff |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Long a portfolio of stocks highly correlated with the S&P 100 | Provides the underlying exposure |
| 2 | Write out-of-the-money calls on the S&P 100, notional roughly equal to the equity portfolio | Creates a ceiling. As stocks rise, portfolio gains are offset by the rising liability of the short call |
| 3 | Buy out-of-the-money puts on the S&P 100, notional roughly equal to the equity portfolio | Creates a floor. Declines are offset by gains on the puts once prices fall below the strike |

Collars are often used to take advantage of option skew, a condition in which call premiums are higher than comparable put premiums, which lets the investor reduce the overall cost of hedging. Madoff claimed the portfolio was held in cash most of the time and that the strategy was implemented over short horizons, typically under 30 days.

Statement (d) is therefore wrong in a specific and instructive way: there is no long call in the structure. The call is sold, and its function is to cap gains rather than to supplement them.

a.reason: Step 2. The call is written out of the money. Correct as stated; not the answer.

b.reason: Step 3. The long put creates the floor. Correct as stated; not the answer.

c.reason: Step 1, and the correlation with the S&P 100 is what makes the index options an effective hedge. Correct as stated; not the answer.

d.reason: This is the answer. The call position is short, not long, and it produces a ceiling rather than supplementary gains.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP on the direction of the call leg, inside a negative qualifier. The structure has exactly one short leg and one long leg among its options, so an item can be built by flipping either, and the sold call is the one flipped here because "gains supplemented by gains" reads as an attractive description of a strategy that reported implausibly steady profits. Recite the collar in terms of its two bounds: the short call is the ceiling, the long put is the floor. Any statement in which the call adds to the upside has the sign wrong.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
questions.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
questions.question: When comparing the returns reported by Madoff's feeder funds with those of the S&P 100, the reported returns were:

options.text: significantly higher than the S&P 100, and more volatile.
significantly higher than the S&P 100, and much less volatile.
approximately the same as the S&P 100, but with much lower volatility.
significantly lower than the S&P 100, but as stable as short-term Treasury bills.

questions.solution:
| Dimension | Reported | Why it was or was not a red flag |
|---|---|---|
| Annual return | Steady 8% to 12% | Comparable in magnitude to the S&P 100. Not implausible on its own, which is precisely why the scheme survived scrutiny. |
| Volatility | Dramatically lower than the S&P 100 | The core statistical impossibility. |
| Down months | Fewer than 5% of all months over a 17-year history | More than 95% of months positive. |
| Down years | None, ever | The single most significant red flag. A split-strike conversion strategy can be profitable over time but will inevitably produce some negative months. |

The distinction matters for how the fraud should have been detected. A manager claiming spectacular returns invites scrutiny. Madoff claimed ordinary returns delivered with extraordinary smoothness, which reads as competence rather than as impossibility until the volatility is examined.

Investors rationalised the consistency in three ways: superior stock selection, the use of market-making profits to smooth reported results, and leverage. Some speculated that Madoff was front running, which is illegal in the United States. None of these could account for the results; the strategy was effectively a black box.

a.reason: Wrong on both dimensions. Returns were comparable rather than significantly higher, and volatility was far lower rather than higher.

b.reason: Correct on volatility, wrong on return level. This is the most attractive distractor because it matches the popular impression of Madoff as a spectacular performer, which the record does not support.

c.reason: Comparable returns, much lower volatility.

d.reason: Reverses the return comparison. Returns of 8% to 12% were not significantly lower than the index.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP on the return dimension at (b) and (d), with the volatility dimension left correct in (b) so that half the option checks out. The narrative pull is the real trap: the popular account of Madoff emphasises enormous fraud, and enormous fraud suggests enormous claimed returns. Fixing the two dimensions separately is the discipline, and the sentence to carry is that the returns were plausible and the smoothness was not.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
questions.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
questions.question: A compliance training module covers the history of Bernard L. Madoff Investment Securities. Which of the following statements about the firm's history and collapse is most accurate?

options.text: The firm began in 1960 as an investment advisory business and later added a brokerage arm, which was the source of its eventual collapse.

The firm began in 1960 as a brokerage business quoting bid and ask prices and executing over-the-counter trades, later adopting electronic trading and eventually expanding into the investment advisory business that collapsed.
The scheme was uncovered by an SEC examination in December 2008 following repeated warnings from a former portfolio manager.
Investors in the feeder funds were able to conduct direct due diligence on the firm itself, but chose not to exercise that right.

questions.solution:
| Fact | The record |
|---|---|
| Origin | Founded in 1960 as a brokerage business quoting bid and ask prices and executing over-the-counter trades. It later adopted electronic trading through the Cincinnati Stock Exchange and eventually expanded into an investment advisory business, which became the source of the collapse. |
| Discovery | Not uncovered by investigation. As markets fell through 2008, redemption requests surged and could not be met. On 10 December 2008 Madoff admitted to his sons, wife and brother that the advisory business was a giant Ponzi scheme. That evening his sons reported him; he was arrested the following day. |
| Due diligence barrier | Capital providers could conduct due diligence only on the feeder funds, not on the firm itself. Madoff did not permit investors to visit his offices, ask questions or interact with him directly, so investors had to rely on the feeder funds to perform the assessment. |

On the warnings point, option (c) contains a real element misassembled. Harry Markopolos, a former portfolio manager, did repeatedly warn the SEC, arguing in his 2005 report *The World's Largest Hedge Fund Is a Fraud* that the returns were impossible without either front running or a Ponzi structure. Regulators dismissed his warnings, and a few banks declined to do business with the firm on their own initiative. The warnings existed; the discovery did not follow from them.

Madoff did not confess out of remorse. Had the market downturn not intensified, the scheme might have continued. The parallel drawn in the source is with the subprime crisis: the structure could persist only while asset prices were rising.

a.reason: Reverses the sequence and therefore the location of the fraud. Brokerage came first; the advisory business came later and was what collapsed.

b.reason: Origin, the electronic-trading development and the later advisory expansion all in the correct order.

c.reason: The warnings are real and the date is right, but the causal chain is wrong. The scheme ended in a confession forced by redemption pressure, not in a regulatory examination. This is the highest-value fact in the whole narrative for exam purposes.

d.reason: Inverts the structural constraint. Investors were unable to conduct that assessment; on-site due diligence was denied or heavily restricted and Madoff refused to answer questions about the strategy. Framing it as a right they declined to exercise misplaces the responsibility onto the investors.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (a) on the order of the two businesses, and at (d) on whether direct due diligence was available. ROLE MISASSIGNMENT at (c), which credits the discovery to the regulator when the regulator had in fact dismissed the warnings it received. That option is the most tempting because every element in it is individually true, and only the causal link is fabricated. Where an option assembles real facts into a chain, test the link rather than the facts.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
questions.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
questions.question: An analyst is separating the investment red flags in the Madoff case from the operational ones. Which of the following is an investment red flag, meaning one revealing an inconsistency between the reported strategy and the reported performance?

options.text: A small three-person audit firm oversaw USD 17 billion in assets.
The firm charged no management or performance fees, collecting only brokerage commissions on trades.
Form 13F filings showed holdings in small, non-S&P 100 companies, inconsistent with the claimed strategy focus.
Feeder funds were prohibited from naming the firm in their marketing materials and offering documents.

questions.solution:
| Category | Members |
|---|---|
| Operational — how the firm was run | Lack of independent oversight, with nearly all key functions performed internally; conflict of interest, acting as both broker-dealer and market maker; a three-person audit firm for USD 17 billion; family control of senior positions; an unusual fee structure charging no management or performance fees; lack of transparency and restricted communication; late SEC registration, only in 2006; and reliance on mailed paper trade confirmations rather than electronic account access. |
| Investment — whether the trades were real | Black box strategy: unrealistically consistent returns with no down months. Questionable style exposure: quantitative style analysis showed exposure patterns opposite to what a split-strike conversion would generate. Illogical Form 13F filings: holdings in small non-index firms contradicting the stated S&P 100 focus. Impossible use of S&P 100 options: the scale of alleged trading was implausible given the illiquidity of those options and the absence of identifiable counterparties. |

Option (c) is the Form 13F flag. Madoff explained the inconsistency by claiming he converted the portfolio to cash at the end of each quarter to avoid public scrutiny of his positions, but moving such sums quarterly would have been impractical and implausible at that scale.

The options flag is the most decisive of the four. Madoff claimed to use S&P 100 rather than S&P 500 options, which would have been prohibitively expensive and virtually impossible, as those options are less liquid and less widely traded. With USD 17 billion under management his trades would have moved the market noticeably, and no such movements were observed. His claim to trade over the counter does not survive either: counterparties would have suffered losses year after year, faced enormous credit exposures, and needed to hedge, and no evidence of any of this exists.

a.reason: A genuine red flag, but operational. It concerns the credibility of the firm's oversight, not the plausibility of its reported trades.

b.reason: Also genuine and also operational. Forgoing millions in management fees made no economic sense given the purported success, and it allowed feeder funds to charge high fees to their own investors, which likely encouraged them to overlook other warning signs.

c.reason: An investment red flag: the disclosed holdings contradicted the stated strategy, which is an inconsistency between reported strategy and reported activity.

d.reason: Operational, falling under lack of transparency and restricted communication.

trap.explanation: SCOPE ERROR is the operator throughout: every option is a genuine red flag from the same case, and three are simply in the wrong category. Nothing can be eliminated as false. The discriminator to fix before reading the options is that operational flags describe governance and structure, while investment flags describe an inconsistency between the stated strategy and the reported numbers. Applying that test, only (c) references the strategy at all.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the key advantage of the market-driven scenario approach compared with traditional stress testing methods used before the Global Financial Crisis of 2007 to 2009? The MDS approach:

options.text: removes subjectivity entirely by relying on fully automated statistical models.
relies solely on historical relationships between market variables to estimate profit and loss impacts.
eliminates the need for covariance matrices by focusing only on individual asset-level shocks.
provides a structured framework for aggregating diverse expert opinions into forward-looking scenarios.

questions.solution:
| Era | How stress testing worked | What went wrong or improved |
|---|---|---|
| Pre-GFC | Stress testing was an add-on to statistical models such as VaR or ex ante tracking error, with model-consistent stress tests, all depending heavily on historical data. | During the crisis, historical relationships between key market variables broke down entirely, rendering the models unreliable. |
| MDS | Scenario analysis allowing estimation of forward-looking events, with a structured framework that gathers input from a diverse group of investment professionals across asset classes, regions and areas of expertise, which the risk management department then aggregates centrally. | Addresses the absence of an established framework for constructing scenarios, which was the main obstacle to using scenario analysis. |

The framing is important. Scenario analysis had always been available as an alternative to historical models; the barrier was that there was no established framework for constructing scenarios, which left the exercise arbitrary. MDS supplies the framework and reduces subjectivity, but does not eliminate it.

a.reason: Absolute claim. The approach is explicitly described as containing an element of subjectivity, and its value comes from making that subjectivity transparent and challengeable rather than from removing it. It is also not automated: expert judgement is the input.

b.reason: Describes the pre-crisis approach whose failure motivated MDS. Sole reliance on historical relationships is the defect, not the advantage.

c.reason: The covariance matrix is central to MDS, not eliminated by it. Shocks to policy variables are passed through a covariance matrix which is reviewed for plausibility, and the choice of that matrix materially changes the resulting z-scores.

d.reason: Names both defining features: a structured aggregation framework, and forward-looking scenarios rather than historically calibrated ones.

trap.explanation: ABSOLUTE-CLAIM TRAP at (a), on the word "entirely", and it is the most attractive distractor because reducing subjectivity genuinely is one of the approach's stated purposes. POLARITY FLIP at (b), which offers the old method as the new advantage. SCOPE ERROR at (c), removing a component the framework depends on. When a stress-testing option claims a method eliminates judgement, treat it as almost certainly wrong: every scenario framework in this syllabus retains judgement and structures it.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
questions.question: The MDS approach is justified by reference to James Surowiecki's argument that decision making improves when information is aggregated from many individuals, subject to three criteria. Which of the following is NOT one of those criteria?

options.text: Each individual should possess specialised knowledge that is not available to others.
Individual opinions must be independent and not influenced by groupthink.
The individuals contributing must have comparable levels of seniority, so that no single view carries disproportionate weight.
There must be an objective mechanism for aggregating private views into a collective assessment.

questions.solution:
| Criterion | How MDS satisfies it |
|---|---|
| 1. Each individual possesses specialised knowledge not available to others | Input is gathered from a diverse group of investment professionals across asset classes, regions and areas of expertise. |
| 2. Opinions must be independent and not influenced by groupthink | Views are collected privately before aggregation, rather than formed in a room together. |
| 3. An objective mechanism must exist for aggregating private views into a collective assessment | The risk management department develops a centralised process to aggregate the ideas, and statistical tools such as the Mahalanobis distance constrain and refine them. |

Option (c) sounds adjacent to criterion 2, since both concern undue influence, but it says something different and weaker. Surowiecki's requirement is independence of opinion, not equality of rank. A crowd of equally senior people who talk each other into a consensus violates criterion 2; a group of unequal seniority whose views are collected independently satisfies it.

The parallel with LO 7 is worth noting. Insufficient questioning, reason 7 on the hedge fund failure list, is exactly criterion 2 failing inside an investment committee: a dominant member sways the decision, and independence of opinion is lost. The remedy in both cases is procedural, namely to elicit views before the group converges.

a.reason: Criterion 1, stated in its own terms.

b.reason: Criterion 2, including the explicit reference to groupthink.

c.reason: Not a criterion. Comparable seniority is neither necessary nor sufficient for independence of opinion, and diversity of expertise, which criterion 1 requires, often implies differences in rank.

d.reason: Criterion 3, and the one MDS operationalises through the centralised risk management process.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP between independence of opinion and equality of status, which is a genuinely fine distinction and a plausible-sounding substitution. The fabricated criterion is also the only one that would be difficult to implement in practice, which is a useful heuristic: a criterion that a real risk department could not satisfy is unlikely to be in a framework designed for real risk departments.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
questions.question: A risk manager is documenting the steps of the market-driven scenario process for her firm's stress testing policy. Which of the following most accurately describes how the process runs?

options.text: Risk managers, investors and economists identify a current issue; idealised outcomes covering a broad spectrum are defined; those outcomes are translated into instantaneous shocks on policy variables; the shocks are assessed for plausibility and passed through a covariance matrix; the scenario is refined over several iterations; the finalised shocks are run through a valuation engine to produce a portfolio profit and loss.

The portfolio is first run through a valuation engine to identify its largest exposures; shocks are then designed to target those exposures specifically; the resulting scenario is accepted without further iteration, since it is by construction the worst case for that portfolio.

Historical crisis episodes are ranked by severity; the most severe is selected; its realised shocks are applied unchanged to the current portfolio; the resulting profit and loss becomes the stress result.

Shocks are applied to every risk factor simultaneously and independently; a covariance matrix is then fitted to the resulting perturbation vector; the scenario is accepted if the fitted matrix matches the historical one.

questions.solution:
| Step | Action | Why it sits here in the sequence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Periodically identify current issues that could affect financial markets, such as inflation, trade policy or monetary policy | The scenario originates in a view about the world, not in the portfolio. |
| 2 | Define a set of idealised outcomes covering a broad spectrum of plausible possibilities | Requires creativity; the statistical tools come later to constrain and refine. |
| 3 | Translate outcomes into instantaneous shocks on policy variables such as equity, bond or commodity indices | Converts a narrative into a quantitative perturbation. |
| 4 | Assess plausibility and magnitude using the Mahalanobis distance; pass the shocks through a covariance matrix, reviewed for plausibility | This is where the statistical discipline enters and constrains the creative step. |
| 5 | Refine through several iterations until a collective version is agreed | The iterative feedback loop is described as an essential component of effective portfolio risk management. |
| 6 | Enter the finalised shocks into a valuation engine and apply them to the portfolio, producing a profit and loss that identifies key underlying risk drivers | The portfolio enters only at the end, which is what keeps the scenario honest. |

The ordering carries the methodology's central discipline: the scenario is constructed from a view about markets and constrained by statistics, and only then confronted with the portfolio. Reversing that, as option (b) does, produces a scenario reverse-engineered to the book being tested.

a.reason: All six steps in the stated order, including the iteration before valuation.

b.reason: Inverts the sequence so that the portfolio drives the scenario, and removes the iteration. A scenario designed against known exposures tells you what you already suspected and cannot surface the unanticipated risk drivers the method exists to find.

c.reason: Describes historical scenario replay, which is precisely the pre-crisis approach that failed when historical relationships broke down. MDS is forward looking; history enters only through the risk ruler as a calibration reference, not as the scenario itself.

d.reason: Reverses the role of the covariance matrix. It is an input used to imply the non-policy shocks and to assess plausibility, not something fitted to a scenario after the fact. Shocking every risk factor independently also contradicts the conditional structure, in which a small set of policy variables is shocked and the rest are implied.

trap.explanation: ROLE MISASSIGNMENT at (b) and (d), applied to the order of operations: in (b) the portfolio takes the role of the scenario's origin, and in (d) the covariance matrix becomes an output rather than an input. SIBLING SWAP at (c), substituting historical replay for a forward-looking framework. The diagnostic question for any process item: what is the first input, and what is the last output? Here it runs from a macroeconomic issue to a portfolio profit and loss, and any option running the other way is wrong.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario (MDS) approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
questions.question: A chief risk officer is asked by her board to evaluate, rather than merely describe, the market-driven scenario approach the firm has adopted. Which of the following is the most appropriate evaluation?

options.text: The approach is unsound, because any framework retaining an element of subjectivity cannot produce a defensible stress result.

The approach retains an element of subjectivity, and that is precisely where its value lies: it forces risk takers through a structured process that quantifies their subjective views, which can then be made transparent, challenged and refined.
The approach is sound because the Mahalanobis distance provides an objective test that accepts or rejects each proposed scenario, removing the need for iteration.
The approach is sound but adds little beyond VaR, since both ultimately rely on the same covariance matrix and therefore produce the same tail estimates.

questions.solution:
The source's own evaluation is direct: although this scenario approach contains an element of subjectivity, it remains highly valuable. It requires risk takers to work through a structured process that quantifies their subjective views, and once those views are made transparent they can be challenged and refined. That iterative feedback process is an essential component of effective portfolio risk management.

| Property | Strength | Limitation |
|---|---|---|
| Forward looking | Not tied to historical relationships that break down in crises | Requires judgement about events with no precedent |
| Aggregation of experts | Draws on specialised knowledge across asset classes and regions | Depends on genuine independence of the contributed views |
| Statistical discipline | Mahalanobis distance and z-scores constrain implausible shocks | Results depend materially on the covariance matrix chosen |
| Iterative refinement | Views become transparent and challengeable | Subjectivity is reduced, never eliminated |

The correct evaluation is therefore neither a rejection nor an unqualified endorsement. It is that the method converts private, unstated intuitions into stated, quantified propositions, and a stated proposition can be argued with.

a.reason: Absolute claim. Every scenario framework in the syllabus retains judgement, and a standard that rejects any such framework would reject scenario analysis altogether, which the source explicitly advocates.

b.reason: Acknowledges the limitation and identifies why it is not fatal, which is what an evaluation requires.

c.reason: Overstates what the statistic does. The Mahalanobis distance assesses plausibility and magnitude; it does not produce a binary accept or reject, and the process explicitly proceeds through several iterations until a collective version is agreed.

d.reason: Collapses the distinction the method exists to create. MDS uses the covariance matrix to imply non-policy shocks and to test plausibility, but the scenario itself is a forward-looking view rather than a distributional percentile. It is designed to capture events for which the historical distribution is uninformative, which is exactly where VaR failed in 2008.

trap.explanation: ABSOLUTE-CLAIM TRAP at (a), and the opposite failure, an overclaim of objectivity, at (c). Evaluation questions in GARP-land almost always resolve to a hedged middle position that names both the limitation and the reason it is tolerable, which is the same asymmetry seen throughout: absolute language is disproportionately wrong and hedged language disproportionately right. SCOPE ERROR at (d), which treats a shared input as evidence of an identical output.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
questions.question: A risk manager using the MDS approach wants to determine whether a proposed set of policy shocks is an outlier relative to historical data. Which statistical tool should the manager use?

options.text: Scenario z-score
Volatility z-score
Correlation z-score
Mahalanobis distance

questions.solution:
The four measures. Reference table.

| Measure | What it is | What it answers | Direction convention |
|---|---|---|---|
| Mahalanobis distance | A distance metric accounting for the correlations among data points. Identifies how many standard deviations a point lies from the centre of a distribution, allowing for the shape of the data. The multivariate generalisation of a z-score. | Is this proposed shock vector a multivariate outlier relative to history? | Higher means more of an outlier |
| Scenario z-score | A rescaling of the MD that prevents it from growing at a rate proportional to $\sqrt{n}$ as the number of policy variables $n$ rises. Represents the severity of a scenario in standard deviations. | How severe, and how plausible, is this scenario? | Lower means more plausible. Higher means more severe or less plausible |
| Volatility z-score | The magnitude component, isolated by computing the scenario z-score under the assumption that all correlations between shocks are zero. | How large are the shocks, ignoring how they fit together? | Higher means larger shocks |
| Correlation z-score | The scenario z-score normalised for the magnitude of the shocks. Depends on the signs and relative magnitudes of the individual factor z-scores, not on their absolute magnitudes. | Are these shocks consistent with the assumed co-movement structure? | Close to zero suggests consistency; high positive, above about 1.0, suggests the covariance matrix does not adequately capture the true co-movement |

An implausible shock is one that is highly inconsistent with historical data, that is, an outlier. The most common statistical method for identifying such multivariate outliers is the Mahalanobis distance.

$$MD = f(r, \mu, \Sigma^{-1})$$

where $r$ is the shock vector, $\mu$ the mean vector and $\Sigma^{-1}$ the inverse covariance matrix of policy variables.

The inverse covariance matrix is what makes the measure multivariate rather than a set of separate univariate checks. It accounts for the correlations among data points and identifies how many standard deviations a point is from the centre of the distribution, considering the shape of the data.

The practical importance of the shape adjustment: a shock combination in which equities fall and credit spreads narrow may involve individually unremarkable moves and still be a severe outlier, because the two rarely move that way together. A univariate check on each variable would pass it; the Mahalanobis distance would not.

a.reason: The scenario z-score is a rescaling of the Mahalanobis distance, applied to prevent the MD from growing with $\sqrt{n}$. It measures severity in standard deviations and supports comparison across scenarios; the outlier identification itself is the MD's job.

b.reason: The volatility z-score isolates only the magnitude component by assuming zero correlations, so by construction it discards the correlation information that defines a multivariate outlier.

c.reason: The correlation z-score tests whether the covariance matrix adequately captures co-movement. It is a diagnostic on the model, not a test of whether a given shock vector is extreme.

d.reason: Explicitly identified as the most common statistical method for identifying multivariate outliers.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP across four measures that are all defined within two pages of each other and all expressed in standard deviations, so nothing can be eliminated on units or on plausibility. Option (a) is the strongest distractor because the scenario z-score is genuinely used to judge plausibility, and the discriminator is that the stem asks specifically about outlier detection relative to historical data, which is the MD's stated function. Fix each measure to the one question it answers before reading the options.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
questions.question: An analyst is comparing two proposed scenarios using their scenario z-scores. Which of the following statements about the scenario z-score is most accurate?

options.text: Of two scenarios, the one with the higher scenario z-score is considered more plausible, because a higher score indicates greater consistency with the historical covariance structure.

Of two scenarios, the one with the lower scenario z-score is considered more plausible, and a risk ruler arranges historical events by their z-scores to help assign a score to a hypothetical future event.
The scenario z-score gives the absolute probability of a scenario directly, which is why it is preferred to the Mahalanobis distance.

The scenario z-score is designed to make the Mahalanobis distance grow in proportion to the square root of the number of policy variables, so that scenarios with more variables are penalised appropriately.

questions.solution:
**Direction.** The scenario z-score represents the severity of a scenario in standard deviations. When comparing two scenarios, the one with the lower scenario z-score is considered more plausible. Higher values indicate more severe or less plausible market stresses.

**Purpose of the rescaling.** The measure exists to prevent the Mahalanobis distance from increasing at a rate proportional to the square root of the number of policy variables $n$. Without it, adding policy variables would mechanically inflate the distance and make every richly specified scenario look implausible.

**The risk ruler.** For hypothetical future events, analysts scale subjectively by comparison with past outliers that appeared implausible beforehand and still occurred. A risk ruler provides a spectrum of historical events arranged from most to least plausible, with each carrying its scenario z-score under the selected covariance matrix. An analyst assigns a standard deviation to a hypothetical event by matching its perceived likelihood to one of those historical events.

**Relative against absolute probability**

| What the z-score gives | What it requires |
|---|---|
| Relative probability of events | The assumption that asset returns follow an elliptical distribution. |
| Absolute probability | Additional assumptions. Two routes: a parametric approach assuming a probability distribution for the z-scores, and a nonparametric approach estimating an empirical distribution of z-scores over a historical horizon. |

a.reason: Polarity flip on the direction convention. Higher means more severe and less plausible. The justification offered is also a description of the correlation z-score's role rather than the scenario z-score's.

b.reason: Correct direction and an accurate description of the risk ruler's function.

c.reason: Scenario z-scores measure relative probability under an elliptical distribution assumption. Converting to absolute probability requires further assumptions via a parametric or nonparametric route.

d.reason: States the purpose exactly backwards. The measure exists to prevent growth proportional to $\sqrt{n}$, not to impose it.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP twice, at (a) on the direction of plausibility and at (d) on the purpose of the rescaling, and both are single-word inversions of a true sentence. The direction convention is counterintuitive enough to be worth a Confusables Registry line: with z-scores higher is worse, meaning more severe and less likely, which is the opposite of the reflex that a higher score is better. SCOPE ERROR at (c), promoting a relative measure to an absolute one, which is the same trap the reading flags by naming the two conversion routes.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
questions.question: Kinlaw and Turkington propose decomposing the scenario z-score into two components, one reflecting the magnitude of the shocks and the other reflecting their consistency with the chosen covariance structure. How is the magnitude component isolated?

options.text: By computing the scenario z-score under the assumption that all correlations between shocks are zero.
By computing the scenario z-score under the assumption that all correlations between shocks are one.
By dividing the scenario z-score by the number of policy variables, which removes the dimensional effect of the shock vector.
By computing the scenario z-score using only the largest individual factor shock, since that shock dominates the magnitude of the scenario.

questions.solution:
The scenario z-score conflates two things: how big the shocks are, and how unusual their combination is given the covariance structure. Stripping out the correlations leaves only the first.

| Measure | Correlation structure used | What survives |
|---|---|---|
| Scenario z-score | The full covariance matrix | Magnitude and co-movement consistency together |
| Volatility z-score | All correlations set to zero | Magnitude only. Each shock is measured against its own volatility with no cross-terms. |
| Correlation z-score | Derived by normalising the first for the second | Co-movement consistency only |

Setting the correlations to zero makes the covariance matrix diagonal, so the measure reduces to a combination of each shock scaled by its own standard deviation, with no interaction terms. Nothing about how the shocks fit together can then influence the result, which is exactly the isolation required.

Option (b) would achieve the opposite. Setting all correlations to one imposes a maximally restrictive co-movement structure, which loads the measure with correlation information rather than removing it.

a.reason: Zero correlations remove all cross-terms, leaving magnitude alone.

b.reason: Polarity flip on the correlation assumption. Perfect correlation is the most restrictive assumption available, not the neutral one.

c.reason: Describes a dimensional rescaling, which is the function of the scenario z-score relative to the Mahalanobis distance, not the volatility z-score. Dividing by the number of variables would not remove correlation information.

d.reason: Discards information rather than isolating a component. The magnitude of a multivariate scenario depends on all the shocks, not only the largest, and using one shock would make the measure univariate.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (b), between zero and one, and the two options are otherwise identical sentences. The reasoning that settles it without memorisation: to isolate magnitude you must switch off correlation, and the switched-off value of a correlation is zero. SIBLING SWAP at (c), lifting the scenario z-score's dimensional-rescaling purpose and attaching it to the volatility z-score.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
questions.question: A risk manager computes a correlation z-score of 1.8 for a proposed scenario. A colleague then doubles the size of every individual factor shock in that scenario and asks what happens to the measure. Which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: The correlation z-score doubles, since it scales linearly with the magnitude of the shocks, and a value of 1.8 indicates that the covariance matrix captures co-movement well.

The correlation z-score is unchanged, since it depends on the signs and relative magnitudes of the individual factor z-scores but not on their absolute magnitudes, and a value of 1.8 suggests the covariance matrix may not adequately capture the true co-movement of the shocks.
The correlation z-score is unchanged, and a value of 1.8 suggests the covariance matrix captures co-movement well, since values above 1.0 indicate consistency.
The correlation z-score falls by half, since doubling the shocks raises the volatility z-score in the denominator while leaving the scenario z-score unaffected.

questions.solution:
**Scale invariance.** The correlation z-score normalises the scenario z-score for the magnitude of the shocks, which is precisely what the volatility z-score measures. Because magnitude appears in both the quantity being normalised and the normaliser, it cancels. The correlation z-score depends on the signs and relative magnitudes of the individual factor z-scores, not on their absolute magnitudes. The source states the consequence explicitly: doubling the size of all shocks would not change the correlation z-score. That is what makes it a clean diagnostic on the co-movement structure alone, uncontaminated by how severe the scenario is.

**Interpretation of the level**

| Correlation z-score | What it indicates |
|---|---|
| Close to zero | The shocks are consistent with the covariance matrix. The assumed co-movement structure is doing its job. |
| High positive, for example above 1.0 | The covariance matrix may not adequately capture the true co-movement of the policy variable shocks. The proposed combination is unusual relative to the assumed structure. |

A reading of 1.8 therefore signals a possible problem with the covariance matrix, not a clean bill of health. The practical response is to revisit the matrix, which connects directly to the slow, fast and recent data choices covered in Q41.

a.reason: Wrong on both halves. The measure is scale invariant, and 1.8 is a warning rather than a reassurance.

b.reason: Scale invariance correctly stated with its reason, and the interpretation of a high positive value correctly directed.

c.reason: Correct on scale invariance, wrong on interpretation, and it inverts the threshold: values close to zero suggest consistency, not values above 1.0. This is the most attractive distractor because half of it is right.

d.reason: Assumes doubling the shocks leaves the scenario z-score unaffected, which is false; both the scenario and the volatility z-scores respond to magnitude, which is why the ratio does not.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (c) on the interpretation threshold, embedded in an option whose first clause is correct, which is the classic two-part conjunction structure. The threshold is the fact most likely to be misremembered because the intuition runs the wrong way: with this measure a low number is the good outcome, since it means the model already explains the co-movement. DROPPED TERM at (d), where magnitude is removed from the numerator but left in the denominator.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
questions.question:
A risk team has four questions about a proposed scenario. Which assignment of measures to questions is most appropriate?

| Question | What the team wants to know |
|---|---|
| I | How many standard deviations from the historical centre does this shock vector lie, allowing for the shape of the data? |
| II | How severe is this scenario relative to the 2008 crisis and to other historical episodes? |
| III | How large are these shocks, setting aside the question of whether they fit together plausibly? |
| IV | Does our covariance matrix adequately capture how these variables actually move together? |

options.text: I Mahalanobis distance; II scenario z-score; III volatility z-score; IV correlation z-score
I scenario z-score; II Mahalanobis distance; III correlation z-score; IV volatility z-score
I Mahalanobis distance; II scenario z-score; III correlation z-score; IV volatility z-score
I volatility z-score; II correlation z-score; III Mahalanobis distance; IV scenario z-score

questions.solution:
| Question | Measure | Why it matches |
|---|---|---|
| I | Mahalanobis distance | The phrase "allowing for the shape of the data" is the MD's defining feature: it accounts for correlations among data points and measures distance from the centre of the distribution. |
| II | Scenario z-score | Comparison against historical episodes is exactly what the risk ruler does, and the risk ruler is denominated in scenario z-scores. |
| III | Volatility z-score | "Setting aside whether they fit together" is the zero-correlation assumption that defines the volatility z-score. |
| IV | Correlation z-score | The measure whose high positive value signals that the covariance matrix may not adequately capture true co-movement. |

Note the structural relationship among the four, which makes the assignment memorable rather than arbitrary. The Mahalanobis distance is the primitive. The scenario z-score is the MD rescaled so that it does not grow with $\sqrt{n}$. The volatility z-score is the scenario z-score with correlations switched off. The correlation z-score is what remains when the scenario z-score is normalised by the volatility z-score.

$$MD \to \text{scenario z-score} \to \{\text{volatility z-score}, \text{correlation z-score}\}$$

a.reason: All four assignments follow from the defining feature named in each question.

b.reason: Exchanges the MD and the scenario z-score in I and II, and exchanges the volatility and correlation z-scores in III and IV. Every pairing is a swap between the two measures that are most closely related, which is what makes it superficially coherent.

c.reason: Correct on I and II, then exchanges III and IV. This is the most attractive distractor because the first half checks out, and the remaining swap is between the two derived measures, which are the hardest pair to keep apart.

d.reason: All four misassigned, with the derived measures placed where the primitive belongs.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP applied systematically, and option (c) is the design point: it gets the easy half right and swaps only the volatility and correlation z-scores, which are the pair a candidate is most likely to hold as an undifferentiated blur. The discriminator to fix is a single word each. Volatility is about size. Correlation is about fit. Once that is fixed, III and IV separate immediately.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance, and explain how these are used in estimating the likelihood of occurrence and magnitude of scenarios
questions.question: A risk manager is constructing a market-driven scenario representing a severe equity market crash, and must choose the covariance matrix used to compute the z-scores. Which of the following is the most appropriate guidance?

options.text: Use a long-lookback historical matrix built from normal-market data, because a longer sample gives a more statistically reliable estimate and avoids overfitting to crisis episodes.

Use a matrix estimated from periods that experienced similar crashes, because correlations among risky assets typically spike during crises, and relying only on normal data would understate the severity of the stress.
The choice does not materially matter, because the scenario z-score is normalised for the covariance structure and is therefore invariant to the matrix selected.
Always use the current, most recent covariance matrix, since it incorporates the market's latest information and therefore dominates any historical estimate.

questions.solution:
Choosing the date and parameters used to construct the risk factor covariance matrix significantly affects the resulting z-scores. Three approaches are used in practice.

| Approach | Construction | Character |
|---|---|---|
| Slow data | Historical matrix over a long lookback, for example five years of weekly equally-weighted data before the event | Stable, but slow to reflect regime change |
| Fast data | Historical matrix over a short lookback, for example one year of weekly equally-weighted data before the event | Responsive, but noisier |
| Recent data | The current covariance matrix, which may reflect post-event dynamics | Incorporates what has since happened, which can be an advantage or a contamination depending on the purpose |

Each method changes how surprising a given scenario appears, and each produces a different risk ruler even when evaluating the same set of events. That is the key practical consequence: the same historical episode can carry different z-scores under the three approaches, so a scenario's apparent plausibility is partly a function of the matrix chosen.

The selection rule follows from that. The appropriate choice depends on the scenario being modelled, and for a market crash the matrix should come from periods that experienced similar crashes, because correlations among risky assets typically spike during market crises. Relying only on normal data would likely understate the severity of the stress.

a.reason: Applies a general statistical principle, that longer samples are more reliable, to a case where it fails. A normal-market matrix understates crisis correlations, so it makes the crash scenario look more extreme in z-score terms than it should and misprices the diversification the portfolio will actually have.

b.reason: States the rule and its mechanism, namely correlation spikes in crises.

c.reason: Directly contradicts the reading, which states that the choice significantly affects the resulting z-scores and produces a different risk ruler for the same events. Scale invariance is a property of the correlation z-score with respect to shock magnitude, not of any measure with respect to the covariance matrix.

d.reason: Absolute claim. The recent matrix is one of three legitimate approaches and may reflect post-event dynamics, which can be exactly wrong when the purpose is to assess how surprising an event would have been beforehand.

trap.explanation: SCOPE ERROR at (a), importing a sound general principle into a context that defeats it, and it is the most seductive option because more data really is usually better. ABSOLUTE-CLAIM TRAP at (d) on the word "always". Option (c) is worth logging separately: it borrows the scale-invariance property from Q39 and applies it to the wrong variable, which is a SIBLING SWAP between two different kinds of invariance. The correlation z-score is invariant to shock magnitude; nothing here is invariant to the covariance matrix.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and compare absolute risk, relative risk, policy-mix risk, active management risk, funding risk, and sponsor risk
questions.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
questions.question:
A pension fund has USD 100,000 in assets and USD 90,000 in liabilities. The expected return on the surplus, scaled by assets, is 5% per year, and the annual VaR of the surplus is 22% of assets at the 99% confidence level. Which of the following statements is or are accurate?

I. There is a 99% probability that over the next year the surplus will turn into a deficit of USD 7,000 or more.

II. There is a 1% probability that over the next year the surplus will turn into a deficit of USD 7,000 or more.

III. The surplus VaR is equal to USD 22,000.

IV. The surplus VaR is equal to USD 5,000.

options.text: I only
II and III
II and IV
I and IV

questions.solution:
$$\text{Surplus}_0 = 100{,}000 - 90{,}000 = \text{USD } 10{,}000$$
$$\text{Expected growth} = 5\% \times 100{,}000 = \text{USD } 5{,}000 \ \Rightarrow \ E[\text{Surplus}_1] = 10{,}000 + 5{,}000 = \text{USD } 15{,}000$$
$$\text{Surplus VaR} = 22\% \times 100{,}000 = \text{USD } 22{,}000 \ \Rightarrow \ \text{III is accurate, IV is not}$$
$$15{,}000 - 22{,}000 = -\text{USD } 7{,}000 \ \Rightarrow \ \text{a deficit of USD 7,000 or worse, at the 1\% tail}$$

So II and III hold. Statement I has the correct magnitude with the probability inverted, and statement IV applies the 5% expected return to assets and then mislabels the result as the VaR.

a.reason: Contains only statement I, whose probability is inverted. A 99% confidence VaR describes the 1% tail.

b.reason: Statement II has the right magnitude and the right tail; statement III has the right VaR.

c.reason: Correct on II, then pairs it with IV, which reports the expected growth of USD 5,000 as the surplus VaR.

d.reason: Wrong on both limbs.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP on the probability at statement I, and INTERMEDIATE-RESULT TRAP at statement IV, which offers the expected growth in place of the VaR. Both percentages in the stem apply to assets rather than to the surplus, which is the base error that makes IV superficially plausible. The four options are the complete two-by-two grid over the two pairs, so nothing can be eliminated by shape.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the use of VaR to monitor risk
questions.reading: Reading 88: Jorion, VaR and Risk Budgeting in Investment Management
questions.question: A pension fund allocates USD 4,550 million across different asset classes. The volatility of the investment is 7%. At a 95% level of confidence, what is the value at risk?

options.text: USD 318.5 million
USD 742.11 million
USD 525.53 million
USD 382.20 million

questions.solution:
$$VaR = z \times \sigma \times W = 1.65 \times 0.07 \times 4{,}550 = \text{USD } 525.53 \text{ million}$$
