Terms are negotiated directly and any exchange of financial interests is voluntary. | Depends on voluntary participation, so it can be undermined by holdouts. If too many hold out the restructuring may fail and trigger a costly bankruptcy, leaving everyone worse off. |
| In-court | Binds dissenters through the plan and classification process, so holdouts cannot block a confirmable plan. | Can be time-consuming, costly and damaging to a firm's reputation. |

Option (d) denies something the source states explicitly. A bankruptcy case officially begins when a petition is filed with the bankruptcy court, and there are strategic considerations involved in choosing both the timing of the filing and the jurisdiction. Timing matters because a favourable price on an asset sale is generally easier to obtain before a bankruptcy filing, per LO 95.b, so a firm intending to sell assets has a reason to act first and file later.

Experienced distressed debt investors typically form views on which firms are likely to pursue an out-of-court restructuring or an in-court one, and companies often signal an imminent filing to financial markets, which prepares investors for the likelihood of some financial loss. The choice of route is itself an investable judgment.

a.reason: Both routes with the correct disadvantage attached to each.

b.reason: Reverses the cost and speed comparison. The time and cost burden is attributed to court-supervised restructurings.

c.reason: Invents a procedural precondition. A prepackaged bankruptcy is precisely a filing made with a consensual deal already agreed, which the option's rule would make impossible.

d.reason: Denies the stated strategic considerations over both timing and jurisdiction.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (b) on which route is slower and costlier, and SCOPE ERROR at (c) and (d), one adding a precondition that does not exist and the other removing discretion that does. The prepackaged bankruptcy is the fact that kills (c) and it is worth carrying as a cross-check: it sits at the boundary of the two routes and can be completed in less than six weeks, which is faster than most contested out-of-court negotiations.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and compare different types of equity-based and macro hedge fund strategies and explain their return and risk profiles
questions.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
questions.question: A consultant is describing two equity hedge fund strategies to a pension board. Which of the following is most accurate?

options.text: An equity market neutral strategy targets zero net market exposure so that returns derive from security selection rather than direction, whereas a long/short equity strategy typically maintains a net long bias and therefore retains meaningful market exposure.
An equity market neutral strategy typically maintains a net long bias, whereas a long/short equity strategy targets zero net exposure by construction.
Both strategies target zero net market exposure, and they differ only in the holding period of the underlying positions.
A global macro strategy is a form of equity market neutral strategy, since macro managers hedge all directional exposure through index futures.

questions.solution:
Market neutral is defined by the constraint: the book is constructed so that net market exposure is approximately zero, leaving security selection as the return source. Long/short equity imposes no such constraint and typically runs a net long bias, so part of its return is market beta. That distinction drives the fee fairness test in LO 94.d, since a long/short manager charging performance fees on returns largely produced by net long exposure is being paid for beta.

Global macro is a directional strategy taking positions on macroeconomic developments across currencies, rates, commodities and equity indices, using leverage and derivatives. Directionality is the point, not something to be hedged away.

a.reason: Both definitions with the exposure direction right.

b.reason: Straight exchange of the two profiles.

c.reason: Long/short does not target zero net exposure, and holding period is not the discriminator.

d.reason: Global macro is directional by design.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP at (b). The one-word discriminator: market neutral is a constraint, long/short is a description.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Compare different types of arbitrage strategies and describe the mechanics of convertible arbitrage strategies
questions.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
questions.question: A convertible arbitrageur buys a convertible bond and delta-hedges by shorting the underlying equity. Which of the following best describes the resulting exposure?

options.text: The position is long volatility, since the embedded conversion option gains value as realised volatility rises, and the delta hedge removes first-order directional exposure while leaving the convexity of the option intact.
The position is short volatility, since writing the equity short is equivalent to selling an option on the underlying.
The position is directionally neutral and volatility neutral, which is why convertible arbitrage returns are uncorrelated with all market factors.
The position is long credit risk only, since delta-hedging removes both the equity and the volatility exposure, leaving the issuer's default risk as the sole driver.

questions.solution:
A convertible bond is debt plus a long equity call. Shorting delta shares removes the first-order price sensitivity but not the second-order convexity, so the residual position profits from realised volatility exceeding the implied volatility paid. The arbitrageur also retains credit exposure to the issuer and earns the bond's coupon less the cost of the short.

Book 5 treats the coupon inconsistently across the hedged and unhedged scenarios in its worked example, flagged in the IR Tier audit. Treat the coupon as earned in both.

a.reason: Long volatility with the delta hedge removing direction only.

b.reason: Polarity flip. A short stock position is linear and carries no optionality.

c.reason: Absolute claim, and wrong on volatility. The strategy performed disastrously in 2008 precisely because it is exposed to credit and liquidity factors.

d.reason: Credit exposure is real but not sole. Delta-hedging does not remove gamma.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (b) on the volatility sign. Anchor: you bought the option, so you are long volatility, and no amount of linear hedging changes that.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe the mechanics and risks of event-driven strategies such as merger arbitrage
questions.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the return and risk profile of a merger arbitrage strategy?

options.text: The strategy earns a small, high-probability spread if the deal completes and suffers a large loss if it breaks, producing a return profile resembling a written put and therefore negative skewness.
The strategy earns a large payoff on completion and loses a small premium if the deal breaks, producing positive skewness comparable to a long option position.
The strategy is genuinely market neutral in all states, since the long target and short acquirer positions offset regardless of whether the deal completes.
Deal completion probability is the only determinant of expected return, so the target's pre-announcement price is not required to evaluate the trade.

questions.solution:
The arbitrageur buys the target below the offer price and, in a stock deal, shorts the acquirer. If the deal closes the spread is captured; if it breaks the target typically falls back toward its pre-announcement level, producing a loss far larger than the spread. Many small gains and occasional large losses is the written-option shape, and it means realised volatility understates risk until a break occurs.

$$E(r) = \frac{C \cdot G - (1-C) \cdot L}{P \cdot Y}$$

where $C$ is completion probability, $G$ the gain on completion, $L$ the loss on failure, $P$ the current price and $Y$ the time to completion in years. The denominator annualises the return on capital committed, which is why deal duration matters as much as spread width.

The formula was reconstructed from a worked example and confirmed against a separate released item to four significant figures, per the Final Tier audit.

a.reason: The asymmetry and its option analogy.

b.reason: Reverses the payoff asymmetry.

c.reason: The hedge holds while the deal is live and fails on a break, when the two legs move apart.

d.reason: The pre-announcement price sets L, the loss on failure, and without it the expected return cannot be computed.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (b) on skewness. Anchor: merger arbitrage sells insurance against deal failure.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the mechanics of a distressed securities strategy, and describe challenges, risks and considerations
questions.reading: Reading 90: Stowell & Stowell, Hedge Fund Investment Strategies
questions.question: A distressed debt manager targets the fulcrum security in a reorganising issuer's capital structure. Which of the following best explains this and its principal risk?

options.text: The fulcrum security is the most senior claim expected to be only partially repaid and therefore converted into equity of the reorganised firm; the principal risk is that the valuation of the enterprise proves lower than estimated, pushing the fulcrum higher (to a more senior claim) in the structure and impairing the claim.
The fulcrum security is the most junior claim in the structure, since junior claims offer the greatest upside in a successful reorganisation.
The fulcrum security is identified from the coupon rate, with the highest-coupon instrument being the fulcrum because it carries the greatest cash burden on the issuer.
Distressed investing carries no valuation risk once a Chapter 11 petition is filed, since claim priority is fixed by statute and recoveries follow mechanically.

questions.solution:
The fulcrum is where the enterprise value runs out. Claims senior to it are made whole in cash or reinstated debt; claims junior to it receive little or nothing; the fulcrum itself is partially impaired and typically converted into the reorganised equity, which is how a creditor becomes an owner. Identifying it requires an enterprise valuation, and the whole trade rests on that estimate: if value comes in lower, the fulcrum moves up the structure and the position is impaired.

Other named risks: illiquidity and wide bid-ask spreads; long and uncertain process duration; legal and jurisdictional complexity; and the demands of active participation on creditor committees.

a.reason: Definition and the valuation risk that follows from it.

b.reason: The most junior claim is usually equity, which is generally wiped out.

c.reason: Position in the structure and enterprise value determine the fulcrum, not coupon.

d.reason: Priority is fixed; value is not, and value is what determines where the impairment falls.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP at (b) between fulcrum and most-junior. The fulcrum is a valuation-determined position, and its location moves as the estimate moves.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe different risks faced by investors in hedge funds
questions.question: Which of the following most accurately distinguishes the liquidity restrictions a hedge fund investor may face?

options.text: A lockup prevents redemption for a stated initial period; a gate limits the proportion of fund or investor capital that may be redeemed in any single period; and a side pocket segregates specific illiquid holdings so that they are realised only when the underlying asset is sold.
A gate prevents redemption for a stated initial period, and a lockup limits the proportion redeemable in any period.
A side pocket is a temporary suspension of all redemptions imposed by the regulator during a market stress event.
All three restrictions apply only to offshore feeder vehicles, since onshore partnerships must offer redemption on demand.

questions.solution:
| Restriction | Mechanism | What it protects against |
|---|---|---|
| Lockup | No redemption for an initial period | Early withdrawal before the strategy has time to work. |
| Gate | Caps the proportion redeemable per period | A run. Slows outflows so the manager is not forced to liquidate into a falling market. |
| Side pocket | Segregates specific illiquid holdings | Redeeming investors extracting the liquid assets at inflated marks and leaving the illiquid residue behind. |

The three appear in the partnership agreement, which is why LO 94.b directs the investor to check for limitations or blackout periods on redemptions, and LO 94.d asks whether fund terms are consistent with the strategy. An illiquid strategy without these features is a mismatch.

a.reason: All three as defined.

b.reason: Lockup and gate exchanged.

c.reason: A side pocket is a manager-operated segregation, not a regulatory suspension.

d.reason: These are contractual terms available in both feeders.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP at (b). Anchor on the dimension each restricts: lockup restricts time, gate restricts quantity, side pocket restricts which assets.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain how the activities of hedge funds and exposure to hedge funds can increase systemic risk
questions.question: Which of the following best describes how hedge fund activity can transmit stress to the wider financial system?

options.text: Through leverage obtained from prime brokers, which links fund losses directly to bank balance sheets; through crowded positioning, so that simultaneous unwinding by similarly positioned funds amplifies price moves; and through forced deleveraging, where margin calls compel sales that depress prices and trigger further calls.
Principally through the size of the industry's assets under management, since systemic importance is determined by absolute scale rather than by interconnection or leverage.
Hedge funds cannot transmit systemic stress, since losses fall on sophisticated investors who have accepted the risk and no public money is at stake.
Through their obligation to publish position-level disclosures, which allows other market participants to trade against them during periods of stress.

questions.solution:
Three channels, and all three operated at LTCM. Leverage creates a direct credit link to the banks providing it. Crowding means apparently independent funds hold correlated positions, so a shock hits many at once. Forced deleveraging is the amplifier: margin calls compel sales, sales depress prices, depressed prices trigger further calls. That feedback loop is the same mechanism as the liquidity black hole in the Liquidity book.

Which is why the third regulatory objective under LO 91.c, financial stability, is addressed specifically by limiting leverage and requiring timely and accurate posting of collateral.

a.reason: All three channels.

b.reason: LTCM was small in assets and systemically dangerous through leverage and counterparty linkage.

c.reason: Absolute claim, and contradicted by the inclusion of hedge funds under Dodd-Frank reporting to the FSOC.

d.reason: Hedge funds do not publish position-level disclosures; Form PF is filed with regulators, not the market.

trap.explanation: SCOPE ERROR at (b), substituting scale for interconnection. Systemic importance runs on leverage and linkage, not size.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe characteristics of private credit, including its typical investors and borrowers
questions.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
questions.question: Which of the following most accurately compares private credit with broadly syndicated loans and high-yield bonds?

options.text: Private credit loans are typically bilateral or club deals held to maturity by a small number of lenders, are largely floating rate, are not traded and therefore not marked to market by observable prices, and are extended predominantly to middle-market firms often owned by private equity sponsors.
Private credit loans trade in a liquid secondary market comparable to broadly syndicated loans, which is what allows daily valuation.
Private credit borrowers are predominantly large investment-grade corporates seeking to avoid public disclosure obligations.
Private credit is predominantly fixed rate, which is why the asset class benefited from the rate rises of 2022 and 2023.

questions.solution:
| Attribute | Private credit | Syndicated loans and high-yield bonds |
|---|---|---|
| Distribution | Bilateral or small club, held to maturity | Broadly syndicated or publicly issued |
| Trading | Not traded; valuation by model or appraisal | Secondary market with observable prices |
| Rate basis | Largely floating | Loans floating, bonds typically fixed |
| Borrower | Middle market, often private equity owned | Larger, more established issuers |

The floating-rate feature is what makes option (d) doubly wrong: private credit is floating, and floating-rate lending raised borrower debt service burdens as rates rose, which is a vulnerability rather than a benefit.

a.reason: All four attributes.

b.reason: Absence of a secondary market is the defining feature and the source of the valuation concern.

c.reason: Borrowers are middle-market and typically below investment grade.

d.reason: Floating, and rising rates raised borrower stress rather than benefiting the asset class.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (d) on the rate basis, with a plausible consequence attached. Anchor: private credit is floating rate, so rate rises hurt the borrower.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the return profile and growth profile of the private credit asset class
questions.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
questions.question: Reported private credit returns show higher average returns and lower volatility than comparable public credit. Which of the following best explains this?

options.text: Valuations are infrequent and appraisal based rather than market based, which smooths reported returns and understates true volatility and correlation with public markets; the return premium reflects compensation for illiquidity and credit risk rather than a free lunch.
Private credit managers hedge interest rate and credit spread risk more effectively than public market investors, which genuinely reduces the volatility of the asset class.
Private credit exhibits genuinely low correlation with public credit because the borrowers are unlisted and therefore unaffected by public market conditions.
The lower reported volatility reflects the shorter duration of private credit loans, which mechanically reduces mark-to-market variation.

questions.solution:
The mechanism is the same infrequent-trading and appraisal-valuation problem set out formally in Reading 99. Where prices are not observed, reported returns are stale, and stale returns are autocorrelated, which suppresses measured volatility, beta and correlation. None of that reflects a real reduction in risk; it reflects a failure to observe it.

The consequence for allocation is direct. A mean-variance optimiser fed smoothed private credit inputs will over-allocate, because the asset appears to offer public-market returns at a fraction of the risk. The unsmoothing procedure in LO 99.d exists to correct exactly this.

a.reason: Smoothing as the cause, with the premium correctly attributed to illiquidity and credit risk.

b.reason: Private credit is largely unhedged floating-rate lending to leveraged borrowers.

c.reason: Being unlisted affects observation, not exposure. Middle-market borrowers are highly sensitive to the same macro conditions.

d.reason: Attributes a measurement artefact to duration. The assets are not marked to market at all, so duration is not the mechanism.

trap.explanation: SCOPE ERROR at (c), converting an observation problem into an economic one, which is the single most repeated error across Readings 92, 93 and 99. Not seeing the volatility is not the same as not having it.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and assess the risks and vulnerabilities related to private credit, and explain how private credit can pose risks to financial stability
questions.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
questions.question: Which of the following is LEAST likely to be identified as a vulnerability of the private credit market?

options.text: Deteriorating credit quality and looser underwriting as competition for deals intensifies, including a rising incidence of payment-in-kind arrangements that defer cash interest.
Layered leverage, where leverage exists at the borrower, the fund and the investor level simultaneously, so that a shock is amplified at each layer.
Opacity and stale valuations, which delay recognition of losses and make aggregate exposures difficult for supervisors to observe.
Daily redemption terms across the asset class, which create an immediate liquidity mismatch between redeemable liabilities and illiquid loan assets.

questions.solution:
The dominant private credit vehicle is a closed-end fund with locked capital, which is precisely what makes the asset class less immediately run-prone than an open-ended bond fund. The liquidity concern is real but takes a different form: growth in semi-liquid vehicles offering periodic redemption to retail and wealth investors creates a potential mismatch, and it is the growth of those structures that the source flags, not a market-wide daily redemption feature.

The three genuine vulnerabilities are credit quality deterioration, layered leverage, and opacity with stale valuations, joined by growing interconnection with banks, insurers and pension funds, and by retail participation in a market built for institutions.

a.reason: A named vulnerability. Not the answer.

b.reason: A named vulnerability. Not the answer.

c.reason: A named vulnerability. Not the answer.

d.reason: The answer. Overstates the redemption terms of an asset class dominated by closed-end vehicles.

trap.explanation: SCOPE ERROR at (d), taking a real and growing concern about semi-liquid vehicles and extending it across the whole market. The qualifier is doing the work: growth in semi-liquid structures is the concern, not universal daily dealing.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Assess potential policy recommendations that could help mitigate the risks associated with private credit
questions.reading: Reading 92: IMF GFSR, The Rise and Risks of Private Credit
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the policy direction recommended for private credit?

options.text: A more intrusive supervisory approach centred on closing data gaps through enhanced reporting, monitoring leverage and interconnections across banks, insurers and funds, strengthening liquidity and conduct requirements where retail participation is growing, and improving valuation and stress-testing practices.
Extending the bank capital framework to private credit funds so that they hold risk-weighted capital against loan exposures on the same basis as banks.
Prohibiting retail access to private credit entirely, since the liquidity mismatch cannot be managed through disclosure or structural requirements.
Deferring supervisory action until a credit event materialises, since the absence of realised losses indicates that current arrangements are adequate.

questions.solution: The recommendation is more intrusive supervision built on visibility rather than on capital. The starting problem is that supervisors cannot see aggregate exposures, so data gaps come first, followed by monitoring of leverage and interconnection, targeted liquidity and conduct requirements where retail money is entering, and better valuation and stress testing. Cross-border and cross-sector cooperation is emphasised because the exposures span jurisdictions and regulatory perimeters.

a.reason: The four strands of the recommendation.

b.reason: Imports the bank framework wholesale. The recommendations concern supervision, reporting and conduct, not risk-weighted capital for funds.

c.reason: Absolute claim. The recommendation is stronger safeguards where retail participation grows, not prohibition.

d.reason: Inverts the stance. The concern is precisely that the sector has not been tested through a full default cycle.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP at (b), importing the banking regime into a nonbank policy discussion, which is the standard construction whenever a reading discusses supervision of a nonbank sector.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the motivations for investors to invest in private markets
questions.question: Each of the following is a stated motivation for investing in private markets EXCEPT:

options.text: The potential for higher returns, including an illiquidity premium.
Greater control over the value creation process, through monitoring, guiding and influencing company performance.
Wider geographic and sector reach, including exposure to regions where public markets are underdeveloped, which helps reduce home country bias.
Improved portfolio liquidity, since private funds offer redemption terms negotiated to match the investor's liability profile.

questions.solution: Liquidity is what an investor gives up to access private markets, and the illiquidity premium in (a) is the compensation for giving it up. The two cannot both be motivations. The genuine set covers higher return potential, diversification through low correlation with public markets, control over value creation, wider geographic and sector reach, access to companies never coming to public markets, and exposure to the growth stage of a company's life that public investors miss.

a.reason: A stated motivation. Not the exception.

b.reason: A stated motivation, and the answer to Q8. Not the exception.

c.reason: A stated motivation. Not the exception.

d.reason: The opposite of a private markets characteristic. This is the exception.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP on liquidity, and the internal contradiction with (a) settles it: you cannot earn an illiquidity premium on a liquid asset.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Identify reasons for the failures of hedge funds in the past
questions.reading: Reading 94: Due Diligence for Hedge Funds
questions.question: Studies of historical hedge fund failures find that a majority are attributable to which of the following?

options.text: Operational issues, including misrepresentation of investments, misappropriation of funds, unauthorised trading and inadequate resources, rather than investment losses alone.
Investment losses arising from adverse market movements, which is why market risk measurement is the primary focus of hedge fund due diligence.
Regulatory enforcement action, which forces closure before losses can be realised by investors.
Redemption pressure alone, independent of any operational or investment failure.

questions.solution: This is the finding that justifies the whole of Reading 94. The four named operational categories are misrepresentation of investments, misappropriation of funds, unauthorised trading, and inadequate resources. Investment losses are a genuine cause but not the majority one, and the practical consequence is that diligence effort should be weighted toward operations, which is where LO 94.e is directed.

a.reason: The finding and its four categories.

b.reason: Reverses the finding and draws the wrong process conclusion.

c.reason: Enforcement typically follows a failure rather than causing it.

d.reason: Redemption pressure is a business model risk under LO 94.f and is usually a symptom of a prior problem.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (b), and it is the intuitive answer, which is exactly why the finding is worth carrying: hedge funds fail from the back office more often than from the trading desk.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain different reasons why firms may experience financial distress and identify potential indicators of distress
questions.question: A distressed analyst observes that an issuer's debt is trading well below par. What does the trading level indicate, and how should it be used?

options.text: The trading level reflects the current market price of the firm's debt relative to its full repayment value and serves as an indicator of the market's expectations about distress severity and the range of potential restructuring solutions, so the level itself helps narrow which remedies are realistic.
The trading level reflects only prevailing interest rates, so a discount indicates a rate move rather than any change in the firm's credit condition.
A debt trading level below par indicates that bankruptcy is unavoidable, since the market has already determined that creditors will not be repaid in full.
The trading level is unusable for distressed analysis because private credit and bank debt do not trade, so no observable price exists for any distressed issuer.

questions.solution:
Where a firm's debt is actively traded, the trading level offers insight into the underlying issues and the range of potential solutions. The source pairs debt trading levels with the problems and solutions each implies: a modest discount is consistent with a liquidity problem solvable through refinancing or asset sales, while a deep discount implies the market expects a balance sheet restructuring in which principal is written down.

The conditional matters. The insight is available where debt is actively traded, which is precisely why the private credit valuation problem in Reading 92 is a supervisory concern: no observable price means no early signal.

a.reason: What the level reflects and how it narrows the solution set.

b.reason: Ignores the credit component, which dominates in distress.

c.reason: Absolute claim. A discount is consistent with an out-of-court restructuring, and the source's whole point is that the level distinguishes among outcomes rather than determining one.

d.reason: Overextends a real limitation. The source states the approach applies where debt is actively traded.

trap.explanation: ABSOLUTE-CLAIM TRAP at (c). The trading level is a continuous signal mapping to a range of solutions, not a binary verdict.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the history of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund and describe the fund's reported strategy and its reported performance
questions.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
questions.question: Which of the following describes the strategy Madoff reported using, and why the reported results were implausible?

options.text: A split-strike conversion, holding a basket of large-cap equities while buying puts and selling calls to bracket the return; the results were implausible because the strategy produced remarkably consistent positive returns with almost no down months, whereas a split-strike conversion should track equity markets and lose money when they fall sharply.
A global macro strategy trading currencies and rates through derivatives, whose returns were implausible because macro strategies cannot produce positive returns in trending markets.
A statistical arbitrage strategy whose returns were implausible because the volume of options required was publicly verifiable and matched exchange records.
A convertible arbitrage strategy whose returns were implausible because convertible arbitrage cannot generate positive returns without leverage.

questions.solution:
The split-strike conversion, also called a collar, holds equities, buys protective puts and sells calls to fund them. It is a legitimate strategy with an entirely predictable property: it is correlated with the equity market and loses money when the market falls, with the put limiting the loss rather than eliminating it.

What was reported instead was a smooth positive return series with very few down months across periods including severe equity declines. That pattern is inconsistent with the stated strategy, and the inconsistency was observable from the returns alone. Separately, the options volume required to implement the strategy at the claimed scale exceeded what the market traded, which was verifiable against exchange records.

a.reason: The strategy and the return inconsistency.

b.reason: Wrong strategy, and macro strategies typically perform well in trending markets.

c.reason: Wrong strategy, and reverses the options finding: required volume exceeded market volume.

d.reason: Wrong strategy, and the stated reason is false.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP across strategy names. The transferable lesson: the returns must be consistent with the stated strategy, which is the attribution analysis of LO 94.b applied to a fraud.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Identify characteristics of Bernie Madoff's hedge fund that can serve as warning signs or potential red flags
questions.reading: Reading 96: The Rise and Fall of Bernie Madoff
questions.question: Which of the following was the most significant operational red flag at Madoff's firm?

options.text: The absence of an independent third-party administrator and custodian, with the firm performing execution, custody, administration and valuation itself, and using a three-person audit firm for a purported multi-billion dollar operation.
The fund's use of a large, well-known prime broker, which created concentration risk in a single counterparty.
The fund's high headline fee structure, which was well above industry norms and should have prompted questions about value for money.
The fund's frequent public marketing, which breached the private placement restrictions under Regulation D.

questions.solution:
Self-custody and self-administration is the flag, because it removes every independent check simultaneously. There was no third party holding the assets, none producing the valuations, and none confirming the trades, so the statements investors received were produced entirely by the party they were meant to verify. The audit was performed by a tiny firm with no capacity to audit an operation of the claimed size.

Options (c) and (d) each invert a real feature. Madoff charged no headline management or performance fee on the advisory business, taking compensation through purported commissions, which made the arrangement look cheap and suppressed scrutiny. And the fund was marketed by exclusivity and word of mouth, with access presented as a privilege, which suppressed diligence rather than inviting it.

Investment-side flags ran alongside: implausibly consistent returns, near absence of down months, and options volumes exceeding what the market traded.

a.reason: The self-custody and self-administration structure with the audit inadequacy.

b.reason: Inverts the fact. There was no independent prime broker, which was the problem.

c.reason: Inverts the fee structure. Unusually low stated fees were part of the appeal.

d.reason: Inverts the marketing approach, which relied on exclusivity.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (b), (c) and (d), each stating the opposite of a documented feature. The organising principle: every Madoff red flag is the absence of an independent party, which is why LO 94.e directs the investor to the service providers and their auditors.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and evaluate the market-driven scenario approach used to develop scenarios for stress testing investment portfolios
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the market-driven scenario approach as a conditional stress testing framework?

options.text: Shocks are applied to a small subset of K policy risk drivers, typically major traded instruments such as an equity index, bond yields or factor-mimicking portfolios, and the shocks to the remaining M minus K nonpolicy factors are implied through multivariate regression to generate the full perturbation vector; keeping the number of policy variables small helps minimise arbitrariness in the resulting vector.
Shocks are specified independently for all M risk factors by expert judgment, and the covariance structure is used afterwards to check internal consistency.
Shocks are applied to as many policy variables as possible, since a larger policy set produces a more precisely specified perturbation vector and reduces arbitrariness.
The approach applies a uniform percentage shock across all risk factors, with correlations ignored so that the resulting scenario is conservative.

questions.solution:
The structure is few in, many out. Experts specify shocks to a small number of policy variables, chosen to be major traded instruments whose behaviour is well understood, and the remaining factor shocks are implied by regression from the estimated covariance structure. Estimating the beta coefficients is equivalent to estimating the covariance matrix of the M factor returns.

Keeping $K$ small is the design principle and option (c) reverses it: each additional policy variable is another judgment call, so a larger policy set means more arbitrariness, not less. Positions with embedded optionality and therefore nonlinear payoffs are fully revalued using the perturbation vector rather than approximated linearly.

a.reason: The K against M structure, the regression step, and the small-K rationale.

b.reason: Removes the conditional structure that defines the approach.

c.reason: Reverses the design principle.

d.reason: Discarding correlations is the opposite of the method, and a correlation-blind scenario is not reliably conservative.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (c) on the number of policy variables, with a plausible precision argument attached. Anchor: small K, because every policy variable is a judgment.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe the scenario z-score, the volatility z-score, the correlation z-score, and the Mahalanobis distance
questions.question: Which of the following most accurately describes the plausibility measures used in the MDS approach?

options.text: The Mahalanobis distance is a multivariate generalisation of a z-score using the inverse covariance matrix of the policy variables; the scenario z-score rescales it so that it does not increase in proportion to the square root of the number of policy variables, and when comparing two scenarios the one with the lower scenario z-score is more plausible; the volatility z-score isolates the magnitude component by computing the scenario z-score under the assumption that all correlations between shocks are zero; and the correlation z-score normalises the scenario z-score for shock magnitude.
The scenario z-score measures plausibility such that a higher score indicates a more plausible scenario, since a higher score reflects greater consistency with the historical covariance structure.
The volatility z-score isolates the correlation component by holding shock magnitudes constant, and the correlation z-score isolates the magnitude component by setting all correlations to zero.
The Mahalanobis distance uses the covariance matrix directly rather than its inverse, which is what allows it to be interpreted in standard deviation units.

questions.solution:
| Measure | Definition and direction |
|---|---|
| Mahalanobis distance | A distance metric accounting for correlations among data points, identifying how many standard deviations a point sits from the centre of a distribution given the shape of the data. A multivariate generalisation of a z-score, built from the shock vector, the mean vector, and the inverse covariance matrix of the policy variables. |
| Scenario z-score | Rescales the MD to prevent it increasing in proportion to $\sqrt{n}$, where $n$ is the number of policy variables. Represents scenario severity in standard deviations. Lower means more plausible; higher means more severe or less plausible. |
| Volatility z-score | The magnitude component, isolated by computing the scenario z-score under the assumption that all correlations between shocks are zero. |
| Correlation z-score | Normalises the scenario z-score for the magnitude of the shocks, leaving the component reflecting consistency with the chosen correlation structure. Kinlaw and Turkington (2014). |

Two further points. The risk ruler arranges historical events from most to least plausible with their associated scenario z-scores, letting an analyst assign a standard deviation to a hypothetical event by matching its perceived likelihood to a historical one. And scenario z-scores measure relative probability under an assumed elliptical distribution; converting to an absolute probability requires further assumptions, through either a parametric approach assuming a distribution for the z-scores or a nonparametric approach estimating an empirical distribution over a historical horizon.

a.reason: All four measures with the correct directions.

b.reason: Reverses the plausibility direction. Lower is more plausible.

c.reason: Exchanges the two decomposition components.

d.reason: The MD uses the inverse covariance matrix, which is what standardises the distance.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (b) on the direction, which is the single most testable sentence in the reading, and SIBLING SWAP at (c) between the two z-score components. Two anchors: lower z-score, more plausible, and volatility z-score kills the correlations.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain steps in the process of defining and developing market-driven scenarios
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the sequence for defining and developing a market-driven scenario?

options.text: Define the narrative and identify the policy variables it implies; specify the shocks to those policy variables; assess the plausibility of the proposed shock vector using the scenario z-score and the risk ruler; derive the implied shocks to nonpolicy factors by regression; then compute portfolio impact, fully revaluing positions with nonlinear payoffs.
Compute the portfolio impact first across a wide range of arbitrary shocks, then select the shock vector producing the largest loss and construct a narrative to justify it.
Derive the implied nonpolicy shocks first, then choose policy variable shocks consistent with them, since the nonpolicy factors are more numerous and therefore more informative.
Specify shocks to all factors simultaneously by expert judgment, since regression-implied shocks embed historical relationships that may not hold under stress.

questions.solution:
The order matters because each step depends on the previous one. The narrative comes first and determines which policy variables are relevant. Shocks are then specified for those variables only. Plausibility is assessed before proceeding, using the scenario z-score and the risk ruler, so that an implausible vector is caught before effort is spent propagating it. Only then are the nonpolicy shocks implied by regression, and finally the portfolio impact is computed, with optionality fully revalued.

Option (b) inverts the logic into reverse stress testing, which is a legitimate but different technique: it starts from a fixed bad outcome and searches for scenarios severe enough to cause it. The MDS approach starts from a plausible narrative and asks what it would do to the portfolio.

a.reason: The full sequence with the plausibility gate in position.

b.reason: Describes reverse stress testing, and constructing a narrative to fit a chosen loss is the opposite of the method.

c.reason: Reverses the conditional structure. Nonpolicy shocks are outputs.

d.reason: Removes the regression step. The concern about historical relationships is real and is treated as a challenge under 97.d, not as grounds for abandoning the method.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP at (b) between market-driven and reverse stress testing, the standard pairing in this family. MDS runs scenario to outcome; reverse runs outcome to scenario.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe challenges and considerations that may arise when implementing the market-driven scenario approach
questions.question: Which of the following is the most significant challenge in implementing the MDS approach?

options.text: The implied shocks depend entirely on the estimated covariance matrix, so the choice of estimation window determines the result: a long history embeds regimes no longer relevant, while a short recent window may omit the stress relationships the scenario is designed to capture, and correlations themselves change under stress.
The approach requires the full perturbation vector to be specified by expert judgment, which makes it prohibitively labour intensive for large portfolios.
The approach cannot accommodate positions with nonlinear payoffs, since portfolio impact is computed as a linear function of factor shocks.
Scenario z-scores translate directly into absolute probabilities without further assumptions, which gives users false confidence in the precision of the estimates.

questions.solution:
Everything downstream of the policy shocks is generated from the estimated covariance structure, so the estimation choice is the dominant model risk. The reading notes that the risk ruler can be built using historical data or more recent data, and the two produce different z-scores for the same event. The deeper problem is that correlations change under stress, typically rising, so a covariance matrix estimated in calm conditions will understate the co-movement the scenario is meant to represent.

Other considerations: the subjectivity of expert-proposed shocks, the linearity assumption for ordinary positions, and the need for full revaluation where optionality is present.

a.reason: The estimation window trade-off and the instability of correlations under stress.

b.reason: Reverses the method. Only the small policy set is specified by judgment.

c.reason: Nonlinear positions are fully revalued using the perturbation vector.

d.reason: Reverses the stated position. Converting a z-score to an absolute probability requires additional assumptions, whether parametric or nonparametric.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (d) on whether absolute probabilities come free, and it is the better distractor because it correctly identifies false precision as a concern while misstating the mechanism.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain best practices for managing liquidity risk in an investment fund
questions.question: Which of the following best describes best practice for liquidity risk management in an investment fund?

options.text: Liquidity risk management should be independent of portfolio management, integrated across the investment process from pre-trade through ongoing monitoring, supported by governance with clear escalation, and calibrated to both the liquidity of the assets and the redemption profile of the liabilities.
Liquidity risk should be owned by the portfolio management team, since they hold the most detailed knowledge of the positions and can act fastest.
Liquidity risk management should focus on the asset side alone, since redemption behaviour is driven by investors and cannot be modelled.
Liquidity should be assessed at the point of purchase only, since a security's liquidity characteristics are established at issuance and do not change materially.

questions.solution:
Four elements: independence from the function whose decisions are being constrained; integration across the investment process rather than a periodic report; governance with defined escalation; and calibration to both sides of the balance sheet, since a fund's liquidity risk is the interaction of asset liquidity with redemption terms.

Option (b) is the independence violation and the same error as letting a model development team validate its own models. Knowledge and independence are different properties, and the control rests on the second.

a.reason: All four elements.

b.reason: Role misassignment. The portfolio manager has an interest in the liquidity assessment of positions already held.

c.reason: Denies the liability side, which LO 98.e is devoted to modelling.

d.reason: Liquidity varies materially with market conditions, which is why ongoing monitoring is required.

trap.explanation: ROLE MISASSIGNMENT at (b), the recurring governance operator: whoever takes the risk cannot be the one who measures it.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain potential challenges fund managers face when managing liquidity risk in fixed-income portfolios
questions.question: Which of the following best explains why liquidity modelling is more difficult for corporate bonds than for listed equities?

options.text: Bonds trade over the counter and infrequently, so volume data is sparse and price discovery is poor; a single issuer may have many outstanding lines with different liquidity; and reported volume understates potential capacity, the difference being latent liquidity.
Corporate bond trading is fully reported in real time with no size caps, so the difficulty arises from an excess of data rather than a shortage.
Corporate bonds trade on exchanges with continuous order books, so the challenge is one of interpreting depth rather than of missing observations.
Bond liquidity is stable through time, so a single historical estimate suffices and the challenge is purely computational.

questions.solution:
Three compounding problems. Bonds are over the counter and many trade only sporadically, so the observations needed to estimate volume are missing. A single issuer may have dozens of outstanding lines differing in size, coupon, maturity and covenant, each with its own liquidity, so issuer-level data does not transfer. And observed volume is lower than the market could theoretically support: the gap between observable liquidity and potential capacity is latent liquidity, which can be estimated using tail measures such as the 90th percentile of the ADV distribution.

Trade reporting also carries size caps that mask the largest trades, which are exactly the ones a liquidity model most needs to see. Where a bond has limited data, a cohort of similar securities is used, constructed on characteristics such as option-adjusted spread, duration, yield or bid-ask spread.

a.reason: All three difficulties including latent liquidity.

b.reason: Reverses the data position and denies size caps.

c.reason: Corporate bonds are predominantly OTC without continuous order books.

d.reason: Bond liquidity varies substantially through time, and daily volume variance is high enough that ADV can be a conservative measure.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (b) on data availability. Latent liquidity is the term to carry: observed volume is a floor on capacity, not a measure of it.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe and apply different approaches to model asset liquidity
questions.question: A fund holds a corporate bond position of USD 30 million. The bond's 20-day average daily volume is USD 5 million, and the risk team assumes a market participation rate of 20%. Using the days-to-liquidate approach, how long would it take to unwind the position?

options.text: 1.2 days
6 days
30 days
150 days

questions.solution:
$$\text{Days to liquidate} = \frac{\text{Trade size}}{\text{Participation rate} \times \text{Average daily volume}} = \frac{30}{0.20 \times 5} = \frac{30}{1.0} = 30\ \text{days}$$

The participation rate is the percentage of a security's ADV that can be sold without causing significant market impact. Selling 20% of a USD 5 million ADV means USD 1 million a day, so a USD 30 million position takes 30 trading days, roughly six weeks. That is the number to compare against the fund's redemption terms: a fund offering monthly redemption holding a position that takes 30 trading days to exit has a mismatch.

The estimate is only as good as its three inputs. Trade size is estimated from historical redemption patterns, portfolio leverage and derivatives exposures. The participation rate is inherently difficult to estimate accurately. And ADV is a mean that can be conservative when daily volume variance is high.

a.reason: 30 / (5 / 0.20) = 1.2. The participation rate divided into ADV instead of multiplied.

b.reason: 30 / 5 = 6. Participation rate dropped, assuming the entire daily volume is available.

c.reason: See working.

d.reason: 30 / 0.20 = 150. ADV dropped.

trap.explanation: DROPPED TERM at (b) and (d), each omitting one denominator input, and SIGN ERROR of the inversion type at (a). Direction check: a participation rate below 1 must lengthen the estimate relative to 30/5 = 6 days, which eliminates (a) and (b) before arithmetic.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Identify examples of extraordinary measures that regulators may allow funds to take to meet unanticipated redemption requests
questions.question: Which of the following is LEAST likely to be an extraordinary measure a regulator may permit a fund to use in meeting unanticipated redemptions?

options.text: Suspension of redemptions, permitted where continued dealing would prejudice remaining investors, typically requiring regulatory notification or approval.
Redemption in kind, transferring a pro rata slice of portfolio securities to the redeeming investor instead of cash.
Side pockets or the segregation of illiquid assets, and temporary borrowing to bridge a redemption where permitted by the fund's terms.
Selling the most illiquid assets first to preserve the liquidity of the remaining portfolio, which is the standard first response before any extraordinary measure is sought.

questions.solution:
Statement (d) inverts the redemption waterfall. A fund meeting redemptions works from cash and the most liquid assets first, then progressively less liquid holdings. Selling the most illiquid assets first would realise the worst prices at the worst time and is neither an extraordinary measure nor a standard response.

The genuine measures are suspension of redemptions, redemption in kind, side pockets, gates limiting the proportion redeemable, temporary borrowing, and swing pricing or anti-dilution levies that charge the transaction cost to the redeeming investor rather than to those who remain. Each addresses the same problem: preventing an exiting investor from imposing liquidation costs on the investors left behind.

a.reason: A named measure. Not the answer.

b.reason: A named measure. Not the answer.

c.reason: Both named. Not the answer.

d.reason: The answer. Inverts the liquidation order and is not an extraordinary measure at all.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP on liquidation order, wrapped in a plausible-sounding rationale about preserving remaining liquidity. The counter-argument is decisive: selling illiquid assets under pressure destroys value, which is the outcome every one of these measures exists to avoid.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain approaches to manage and model redemption risk in an investment fund
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the modelling of redemption risk in an investment fund?

options.text: Redemption-at-risk estimates a high percentile of the distribution of net outflows over a horizon, analogous to value at risk applied to the liability side, using historical redemption data segmented by investor type since institutional, retail and intermediated flows behave differently; the redemption waterfall then determines the order in which assets are liquidated to meet it.
Redemption-at-risk uses the mean of historical net flows, since extreme percentiles are unreliable in a series with few observations.
Redemption modelling should treat all investors as a single homogeneous group, since segmenting by investor type introduces estimation error without improving accuracy.
The redemption waterfall liquidates assets in proportion to portfolio weights in all circumstances, since pro rata liquidation preserves the portfolio's risk profile.

questions.solution:
Redemption-at-risk is a VaR construction applied to liabilities: a high percentile of the net outflow distribution over a chosen horizon. Segmentation by investor type is essential because redemption behaviour differs sharply. Retail flows are numerous and partly offsetting; a single large institutional investor can redeem a substantial share of the fund at once; and intermediated or platform money can move as a block on a distributor's decision. Concentration in the investor base is itself a risk measure.

The redemption waterfall then sets the liquidation order, working from cash and the most liquid holdings outward. Option (d) describes pro rata slicing, which is a genuine alternative and is precisely what LO 98.c warns about: quickly liquidating assets on a pro rata basis may cause undesirable price effects, because it forces sales of the illiquid sleeve at the worst moment. It preserves the risk profile at the cost of realising the highest transaction costs.

a.reason: The percentile construction, investor segmentation, and the waterfall.

b.reason: A mean cannot measure a tail. The whole purpose is the extreme outflow.

c.reason: Reverses the requirement. Segmentation is what makes the estimate meaningful.

d.reason: States pro rata liquidation as universal. It is one approach with a documented drawback.

trap.explanation: SIBLING SWAP at (d) between waterfall and pro rata liquidation, with a true justification attached. Note the parallel with the asset side: this is the same trade-off as the equal-split against front-loaded unwind schedule in the Liquidity book.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the characteristics of illiquid markets
questions.question: Which of the following best characterises illiquid asset markets?

options.text: Illiquid markets comprise a large share of aggregate wealth, including real estate, private equity, private debt, infrastructure and institutional-quality collectibles; they are characterised by infrequent trading, large transaction costs, small numbers of investors and long periods between trades.
Illiquid markets are a small and specialised segment of aggregate wealth, which is why illiquidity is treated as a niche consideration in portfolio construction.
Illiquidity is a permanent characteristic of a market, so a market that is liquid today can be relied upon to remain liquid in a crisis.
Illiquid markets are defined by wide bid-ask spreads alone, with trading frequency and investor participation being incidental.

questions.solution:
Ang's opening point is that illiquid markets are not a niche: they account for a large proportion of aggregate wealth, and most investors hold their largest single asset, a house, in one. The characteristics are infrequent trading, large transaction costs, small numbers of investors, and long periods between transactions.

Option (c) is the one worth rejecting deliberately. Liquidity dries up, and it does so precisely in crises: markets that traded continuously can cease functioning, which is why liquidity risk is a state-dependent property rather than a fixed label. That is the liquidity black hole mechanism from the Liquidity book expressed in an asset allocation setting.

a.reason: Both the scale point and the four characteristics.

b.reason: Reverses the scale point.

c.reason: Liquidity dries up in crises; it is not permanent.

d.reason: Reduces a multi-attribute definition to one attribute.

trap.explanation: ABSOLUTE-CLAIM TRAP at (c) on permanence, which contradicts the reading's most practically important observation.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Discuss the relationship between market imperfections and illiquidity
questions.question: Which of the following correctly identifies the market imperfections that give rise to illiquidity?

options.text: Clientele effects and participation costs; transaction costs including search costs; asymmetric information, where informed traders make market makers reluctant to trade; funding constraints affecting leveraged investors; and search frictions in markets where a counterparty must be found rather than met on an exchange.
Illiquidity arises solely from the physical indivisibility of the underlying assets, which is why real estate is illiquid and securities are not.
Illiquidity arises from regulation alone, so removing regulatory restrictions would render all asset markets equally liquid.
Asymmetric information increases liquidity, since informed traders provide price discovery that narrows spreads and encourages market makers to quote.

questions.solution:
Ang names six imperfections: clientele effects and participation costs, transaction costs, search frictions, asymmetric information, price impact (imperfect competition), and funding constraints. Option (a) lists five of them (it omits price impact), and every clause it states is accurate. The one most often reversed is asymmetric information: a market maker who suspects the counterparty knows more will widen the spread or withdraw, because trading against an informed counterparty is a losing proposition on average. Adverse selection reduces liquidity, and option (d) inverts exactly this.

Search frictions are the defining feature of over-the-counter markets, where a buyer must be located rather than met on an exchange, which is why the days-to-liquidate framework in LO 98.c matters for bonds and not for listed equities.

a.reason: Five of the six named imperfections, each stated correctly (price impact omitted).

b.reason: Divisible securities can be highly illiquid; indivisibility is not the mechanism.

c.reason: Absolute claim naming one source and excluding the rest.

d.reason: Reverses the effect. Adverse selection widens spreads.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (d), and the argument offered is superficially reasonable. The test: would you quote a tight price to someone who knows more than you?

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Assess the impact of biases on reported returns for illiquid assets
questions.question: Reported returns on illiquid assets are subject to three biases. Which of the following correctly describes them and their combined effect?

options.text: Survivorship bias, since failed funds and assets drop out of the reported sample; selection bias, since assets tend to be transacted and reported when their prices are high; and infrequent trading, which smooths reported returns; together they overstate returns and understate risk, so reported Sharpe ratios are flattered from both directions.
The three biases work in offsetting directions, so their net effect on reported Sharpe ratios is approximately neutral.
Selection bias causes assets to be reported when prices are low, which understates reported returns and makes illiquid assets appear less attractive than they are.
Infrequent trading affects reported volatility but leaves reported beta and correlation unaffected, since those are estimated from the same return series.

questions.solution:
| Bias | Mechanism | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Survivorship | Failed funds and assets leave the sample | Overstates returns |
| Selection | Assets are transacted and reported when prices are high; sellers withhold in weak markets | Overstates returns |
| Infrequent trading | Stale prices produce autocorrelated returns | Understates volatility, beta and correlation |

The two directions compound. Returns are inflated and risk is suppressed, so every risk-adjusted measure built from reported data is flattered twice, and a mean-variance optimiser fed those inputs will over-allocate to the asset class.

Option (d) is the sharpest distractor and is false: infrequent trading damages beta and correlation estimates most of all, because those depend on the co-movement between the asset and the market at a given point in time, and stale prices destroy the timing alignment entirely.

a.reason: All three biases and the compounding effect.

b.reason: They reinforce rather than offset.

c.reason: Reverses selection bias.

d.reason: Beta and correlation are the estimates smoothing damages most.

trap.explanation: SCOPE ERROR at (d), limiting smoothing to volatility. Registry line: selection biases inflate the numerator, smoothing deflates the denominator, and both flatter the Sharpe ratio by opposite routes. POLARITY FLIP at (c), reversing the direction of selection bias.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain the process of unsmoothing returns and the effects of unsmoothing
questions.question: An analyst applies the Geltner-Ross-Zisler unsmoothing procedure to a series of reported private real estate returns. Which of the following describes the effect?

options.text: Unsmoothing removes the autocorrelation induced by stale pricing, which raises estimated volatility and raises estimated correlation and beta with public markets, while leaving the mean return approximately unchanged; the asset therefore looks substantially less attractive on a risk-adjusted basis, though the true underlying risk has not changed.
Unsmoothing lowers estimated volatility, since removing noise from a return series reduces its dispersion.
Unsmoothing raises both the estimated mean return and the estimated volatility, since correcting stale prices reveals returns that were previously unreported.
Unsmoothing raises estimated volatility but leaves estimated correlation with public markets unchanged, since correlation is scale invariant.

questions.solution:
Observed returns are a weighted average of current and past true returns, which induces positive autocorrelation. Reversing that filter recovers a series with higher volatility and higher correlation and beta to public markets. The mean is approximately unchanged, because averaging redistributes returns across periods without changing their sum.

$$\sigma_{true} = \sigma_{observed} \times \sqrt{\frac{1+\varphi}{1-\varphi}}$$

where $\varphi$ is the first-order autocorrelation of the reported returns. It follows from the unsmoothing filter $r_t = (r^*_t - \varphi r^*_{t-1})/(1-\varphi)$: $var(r_t) = var(r^*_t)\,(1+\varphi^2-2\varphi^2)/(1-\varphi)^2 = var(r^*_t)\,(1+\varphi)/(1-\varphi)$. At $\varphi = 0.50$ the multiplier is $\sqrt{1.5/0.5} = \sqrt{3} = 1.732$, so a reported 9% volatility becomes 15.59%. At $\varphi = 0$ the multiplier is 1 and nothing changes, which is the sanity check.

Caution: some study materials (including the source of this question and IR-FT-76) print the multiplier as $(1+\varphi^2)/(1-\varphi^2)$, which gives 11.62%. That expression does not follow from the filter. If an exam item states its own formula, use the one it states.

The interpretive point is the one exams test: unsmoothing changes the measurement, not the asset. The risk was always there; it was simply not being observed, and diversification benefits that appeared in the reported data largely disappear once the correlation is corrected.

a.reason: All three effects and the correct interpretation.

b.reason: Polarity flip. Volatility rises.

c.reason: Correct on volatility, wrong on the mean, which is approximately preserved.

d.reason: Correlation rises. The stale pricing destroyed the timing alignment that correlation depends on, and restoring it restores the measured co-movement.

trap.explanation: SCOPE ERROR at (d), getting volatility right and correlation wrong, which is the designed miss because "correlation is scale invariant" is a true statement about scaling and irrelevant to a filter that changes the timing of the series. POLARITY FLIP at (b), reversing the direction of the volatility effect.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Compare illiquidity risk premiums across and within asset categories
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the evidence on illiquidity risk premiums?

options.text: There is little evidence of large illiquidity risk premiums across asset classes, but substantial evidence of illiquidity premiums within asset classes, where less liquid securities earn higher returns than more liquid ones of the same type.
Illiquidity premiums are large and reliable across asset classes, which is the primary justification for allocating to private markets.
Illiquidity premiums exist across asset classes but not within them, since securities of the same type are close substitutes and must therefore offer identical expected returns.
Illiquidity premiums are constant through time, so an investor can capture them equally well at any point in the cycle.

questions.solution:
The finding is counterintuitive and heavily tested. Comparing illiquid asset classes with liquid ones produces little evidence of a large premium once the reporting biases of LO 99.c are corrected. Comparing securities within an asset class, where the biases apply more evenly, produces consistent evidence: less liquid stocks, bonds and other instruments earn higher returns than their more liquid counterparts.

The practical implication is that the premium is captured by being the liquidity provider within a market rather than by moving wholesale into illiquid asset classes. Premiums also vary through time, rising in crises when liquidity is most valuable, so the ability to supply liquidity when others cannot is where the return sits.

a.reason: The across against within asymmetry as reported.

b.reason: Reverses the across-class finding, and it is the intuitive and widely believed claim.

c.reason: Exactly inverts both halves.

d.reason: Premiums vary through time and rise in crises.

trap.explanation: POLARITY FLIP at (b) and (c). Registry line worth carrying: little across, substantial within. It is the single most counterintuitive result in the Investment Management book.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Evaluate the impact of allocating illiquid assets to a portfolio
questions.question: Which of the following best describes the impact of allocating illiquid assets to a portfolio?

options.text: Illiquidity prevents rebalancing at the desired frequency, so realised weights drift from targets and the investor cannot harvest the rebalancing premium; portfolio choice models suggest allocations should be modest and should account for the investor's inability to trade, and the investor must rely on manager talent while facing difficulties monitoring external managers.
Illiquid assets improve rebalancing discipline, since the inability to trade prevents the investor from making behaviourally driven decisions during stress.
Optimal allocations to illiquid assets are high because reported volatility is low, and this conclusion holds after unsmoothing.
Illiquid asset allocations require no adjustment for the investor's liability profile, since the illiquidity premium compensates for all timing mismatches.

questions.solution:
Three consequences. Rebalancing becomes impossible at the desired frequency, so weights drift and the rebalancing premium available to a liquid portfolio is forgone. Portfolio choice models incorporating illiquidity produce modest optimal allocations, well below what naive mean-variance optimisation on reported data suggests. And the investor must rely on manager talent while facing genuine difficulty monitoring external managers, which connects to the selection risk asymmetry in LO 93.d.

Option (c) fails on the second clause, which is where the item is decided. Optimal allocations do look high on reported data, and that is precisely the artefact unsmoothing removes. Any conclusion surviving "after unsmoothing" must be built on the corrected inputs.

a.reason: All three consequences.

b.reason: Inverts a constraint into a benefit. Forced inaction is not discipline, and it prevents the investor from selling when circumstances require it.

c.reason: True premise, false conclusion. Unsmoothing is what destroys the high allocation.

d.reason: Absolute claim. Matching illiquid holdings to the liability profile is central, which is the endowment against pension distinction.

trap.explanation: SCOPE ERROR at (c), a true observation carried past the correction that reverses it, and it is the harder build because it explicitly names unsmoothing. Grade the clause after the connective: the conclusion is where the option fails, not the premise.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain how different risks can arise for investors in private markets and assess how these risks can be measured
questions.question: An endowment holds USD 700 million in public equities and USD 300 million in private equity, against a 30% target weight for private equity. Public equities fall 30% over a quarter. No capital is called or distributed, and the private equity holdings carry their prior quarter-end valuation. What is the reported private equity weight after the fall?
questions.solution:
| Component | Before | After | Why |
|---|---|---|---|
| Public equities | 700 | 490 | Marked to market, down 30%. |
| Private equity | 300 | 300 | Stale. No transaction has forced revaluation. |
| Total | 1,000 | 790 | The denominator has fallen. |

$$\text{Private weight} = \frac{300}{790} = 38.0\%$$

against a 30% target, an apparent overweight of 8 percentage points. Not one dollar of private exposure has changed. The entire 8-point drift is an artefact of comparing a stale numerator with a live denominator, which is the denominator effect. An investor rebalancing mechanically would sell private assets into the secondary market at a discount, in the worst quarter, to correct a deviation that does not exist. This is why the source warns that slow-moving private valuations make some weight differences artificial, leading to unnecessary rebalancing.

a.reason: 210/790. Marks the private sleeve down 30% in the numerator but leaves it at 300 in the denominator, an inconsistent mix. Had the private book genuinely been marked down 30% as well, the weight would be 210/700 = 30.0%, the case in which no denominator effect arises.

b.reason: The unchanged target weight, which is what the effect makes impossible to observe.

c.reason: See working.

d.reason: 300/700. Applies the 30% fall to the whole portfolio including the private sleeve, then divides by that reduced total.

trap.explanation: WRONG INPUT TWIN at (d) on which base absorbs the fall. Structural check: the private weight must rise, so any option at or below 30% is wrong before arithmetic.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Explain how a hedge fund's business model risk and its fraud risk can be assessed
questions.reading: Reading 94: Due Diligence for Hedge Funds
questions.question: A hedge fund management company has annual operating expenses of USD 6 million and charges a management fee of 1.5% of assets under management, plus a 20% performance fee. In assessing business model risk, an analyst wants the level of AUM at which management fees alone cover operating expenses. What is that level?

options.text: USD 40 million
USD 300 million
USD 400 million
USD 4,000 million

questions.solution:
$$\text{Breakeven AUM} = \frac{\text{Operating expenses}}{\text{Management fee rate}} = \frac{6}{0.015} = \text{USD }400\text{ million}$$

The performance fee is deliberately excluded, and that exclusion is the whole point of the exercise. The source directs the analyst to calculate the percentage of revenues derived from variable incentive or performance fees precisely because those may not materialise in market downturns, and to assess the gap between management fees and operating expenses. A firm below its management-fee breakeven is dependent on performance to survive rather than merely to prosper, and it will be least able to pay its costs in the year its performance fee is zero.

The figure is then compared to current actual and future projected AUM. A firm at USD 250 million running a USD 400 million breakeven has a structural problem no amount of good performance permanently fixes, and it connects directly to the first named failure mode, a lack of cash and working capital.

a.reason: 6/0.15. The fee read as 15% rather than 1.5%.

b.reason: 6/0.02. A 2% fee substituted for the stated 1.5%.

c.reason: See working.

d.reason: 6/0.0015. A further decimal slip.

trap.explanation: UNIT CONVERSION at (a) and (d), and WRONG INPUT TWIN at (b). Sense check: 1.5% of USD 400 million is USD 6 million, which is the fastest confirmation available.

questions.subject: Investment Risk
questions.loText: Describe methods firms can use to remedy a financial distress situation at different stages of distress and explain the potential implications and challenges to using each method
questions.question: A distressed issuer has USD 300 million of bonds outstanding, currently trading at 62 cents on the dollar. It uses available cash to repurchase USD 50 million of face value in the open market. What is the reduction in the firm's debt obligation net of the cash spent, and is the chosen method appropriate?

options.text: USD 19 million, and an open market repurchase is appropriate because the firm is retiring under 20% of the bonds outstanding.
USD 31 million, and an open market repurchase is appropriate because the firm is retiring under 20% of the bonds outstanding.
USD 19 million, but a cash tender offer would be required because any repurchase must be made available to all bondholders on identical terms.
USD 50 million, and an exchange offer would be the appropriate method given the discount.

questions.solution:
| Item | Amount | Note |
|---|---|---|
| Face value retired | 50.0 | The obligation extinguished. |
| Cash paid, 50 × 0.62 | 31.0 | Bonds are repurchased at a discount in distressed situations. |
| Net reduction in obligation | 19.0 | The discount captured by the issuer. |

Method selection: $50 / 300 = 16.7\%$ of bonds outstanding, below the roughly 20% guidance. Open market repurchases are most effective when the firm intends to repurchase less than about 20% of the bonds outstanding, being simple, fast, low cost and discreet. Above that level the buying pressure moves the price against the issuer and a cash tender offer becomes the appropriate tool, available to all bondholders with strict terms. Discretion matters here: a firm openly bidding for its own distressed debt invites holders to withhold.

One further condition from the source: if the firm also has distressed bank debt trading at a discount, lenders often require that available cash be used first to repay bank debt before turning to nonbank debt. A stem mentioning both would change the answer on method even with the arithmetic unchanged.

a.reason: Both the net reduction and the method test.

b.reason: USD 31 million is the cash paid, an intermediate quantity, not the net reduction.

c.reason: Correct figure, wrong method rule. Open market purchases are made discreetly and are not required to be offered to all holders; that is the defining feature of a tender offer.

d.reason: USD 50 million ignores the cash spent, and an exchange offer is the tool for a firm that lacks cash. This firm is using cash it has.
